source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: A local RAG system becomes more useful when its input can include web pages. The original experiment extended a document-based notebook with Crawl4AI, then used the extracted text in the same retrieval and generation pipeline.

The historical stack combined Crawl4AI, LangChain, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, SQLiteVSS, Ollama, and Llama 3 8B. A short Wikipedia page kept the initial example small enough to inspect in a notebook.
Treat crawling as document preparation

Fetching a page and extracting useful text are separate steps. A successful HTTP response can still leave you with navigation, duplicated sections, or missing content. Read the crawler’s output before splitting it into chunks.
Keep the source URL and collection time with the text. When a page changes, that information helps explain why an answer produced from an earlier snapshot differs from what a reader sees today.
Reuse the retrieval pipeline
The original notebook split extracted text, calculated embeddings, stored them in SQLiteVSS, and ran a similarity search. Retrieved passages then became context for a local question-answering prompt.

body.code:
Web page → extracted text → chunks + source metadata
Chunks → embeddings → vector store
Question → relevant passages → local model response

children.text: The retrieval stage selects text; the model reads that text. Adding a crawler does not make every response current or correct. The collection schedule, extraction quality, and retrieval result still determine which evidence reaches the model.
Check failures where they happen

Inspect one example at each boundary: page to text, text to chunks, question to passages, and passages to answer. If an answer is wrong, this makes it possible to locate the failure instead of repeatedly changing the final prompt.

Web content is input data. Instructions found inside it should not gain authority over your application or its tools. For a question that the collected material cannot answer, the useful response is an explicit gap in the evidence.
The recovered article retains the historical notebook steps. For a new implementation, consult
Crawl4AI’s project
for its current installation and extraction interfaces. Start with the
local RAG foundation
if you have not yet verified retrieval over a simple document.

title: MCP with local language models: host, client, server, and tools
excerpt: Understand where the local model sits in an MCP application and how to test a small tool integration before adding more servers.

source.title: MCP with local language models: host, client, server, and tools
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: MCP connects an application to capabilities exposed by servers. A local language model can participate in that application without becoming an MCP server itself. Keeping those responsibilities separate makes the first integration easier to understand.
The original experiment used Ollama, Qwen 2.5 7B, and mcp-cli to work with filesystem, search, and fetch capabilities. It explored the practical connection between a local model and external tools.
Put the model in the host application
The host manages the user interaction and model workflow. Its MCP client connects to a server. The server exposes tools or other capabilities and performs the work requested through that connection.
The model can propose a tool call, but application code handles its execution and returns the result. See the
MCP architecture documentation
for the protocol’s separation of responsibilities.
Begin with one narrow capability
The historical setup used a filesystem server configured with a specific directory. That is a useful place to start because you can compare the returned file list with the directory yourself.

Confirm that the client can list the server’s tools before involving the model. Then ask for a simple read operation and inspect both the arguments and returned data. A missing tool connection and a model choosing the wrong tool are different failures.
Tool-calling compatibility depends on the model, runtime, and client. The original article’s broad exclusion of reasoning models is not a reliable rule for selecting a current implementation.
Add remote services deliberately

The experiment then added Brave Search and a fetch server. Those tools communicate over the network even when inference runs locally. Search also introduces a provider credential and its own service requirements.

Adding servers expands the application’s reach. It does not prove that the model will select the correct operation or that every available tool should be exposed in every conversation. Keep credentials outside committed configuration and expose only the capabilities the task needs.
The original client code lives in
mcp-cli
. For a larger example, the
REST API integration series
follows the same pattern through a warehouse service, a local model, and a Python agent.

title: Minion and Minions: testing collaboration between local and cloud models
excerpt: A historical experiment with HazyResearch’s local/cloud model collaboration, and the measurements that make its tradeoffs visible.

source.title: Minion and Minions: testing collaboration between local and cloud models
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: A local model and a cloud model can share a task instead of treating execution as an all-or-nothing choice. HazyResearch’s Minion and Minions work explored that design: local computation contributes to a larger reasoning workflow coordinated with a more capable model.

The original experiment ran the project’s Streamlit application and notebook using Ollama alongside a cloud provider. It compared the two protocols on a document containing hotel information and reservation dialogues.
Follow the information exchanged

The useful question is what each participant sees and produces. A model running locally does not make the combined workflow private if prompts, excerpts, intermediate results, or documents are sent to a cloud service.
The
HazyResearch repository

describes the protocols and their implementation. Minion uses interaction between the models; Minions adds task decomposition and aggregation across local work. Inspect the version you run rather than assuming every variant sends the same information.
Use a question with a known answer

The original task asked for a minibar bill from a longer hotel dialogue. This made it possible to compare the returned value against an identifiable passage instead of judging the answer only by its writing quality.

An interesting intermediate result was that one worker returned a room-rate figure while another found the relevant minibar charge. The aggregation step therefore had to distinguish a superficially relevant amount from the amount that actually answered the question.

That example illustrates why a final correct answer alone is not enough to understand the workflow. Inspect which pieces of evidence were extracted, what the workers misunderstood, and how the final model resolved the difference.
Measure the whole run

Record the model names, input document, protocol settings, requests, tokens, elapsed time, and final answer. The historical runs reported different cloud costs, but one small example is not a general savings estimate.

A stronger comparison includes a direct cloud baseline and questions of different difficulty. Extra coordination may be worthwhile for one workload and unnecessary for another. It also consumes local resources even when the provider bill falls.

Use the linked project for current setup instructions. This edition preserves the experiment’s central lesson: examine the actual exchange of data and work before deciding whether hybrid execution improves your application.

title: OpenAI Agents SDK with a local model: make the workflow explicit
excerpt: A planner-and-writer example that separates local inference, search tools, orchestration, and tracing.

source.title: OpenAI Agents SDK with a local model: make the workflow explicit
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: An agent framework can coordinate work even when the model runs outside the framework provider’s infrastructure. The original experiment connected the OpenAI Agents SDK to an Ollama endpoint and used a planner-and-writer workflow to draft a technical article.

The proposed topic was deploying Apache Ignite with Docker and Kubernetes. The output was intended as a draft to edit and refine, which is an important distinction for any generated technical tutorial.
Configure the model explicitly

An OpenAI-compatible endpoint needs the appropriate base URL, model name, and client configuration. Compatibility is not a promise that every provider feature behaves identically. Tool calling and the selected API interface both matter.
The current
Agents SDK model documentation
explains support for other providers and common compatibility issues. Use it when adapting the historical notebook to a current environment.
Give each step a concrete output

The planner in the example could call a search function to collect relevant material and produce an outline. The writer received the previous step’s output and drafted the article. The surrounding Python workflow connected those stages.

body.code:
Topic → search results → planner’s outline
Outline + source material → writer’s draft
Draft → human review and technical verification

children.text: An agent name or role description does not by itself guarantee a useful handoff. Pass the actual output that the next stage needs, and retain source URLs so a reviewer can check claims.
Account for search and tracing

The notebook wrapped DuckDuckGo search as a callable tool. That search still reaches an external service when the language model runs locally. Model execution and tool execution have different data paths.

Tracing is another independent setting. The SDK can export traces; configure or disable that behaviour according to the environment. A local base URL alone does not establish that the complete workflow stays on the machine.
Treat a technical draft as unfinished work

Review commands against the versions and platform the article names. Check that referenced links support the claims, that prerequisites are complete, and that error paths are explained. A second model can help edit the prose, but it cannot substitute for running the tutorial in its intended environment.
The recovered source contains the original notebook and orchestration examples. For the broader content workflow, continue with
local AI content pipelines

title: A2A in practice: a travel planner with separate agent services
excerpt: Follow a historical weather, search, and local-model example to understand discovery, service boundaries, and task coordination.

source.title: A2A in practice: a travel planner with separate agent services
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: The original A2A experiment built a travel-planning workflow from separate services. One agent fetched weather information, another searched for activities, and a local language model turned the gathered material into a readable plan.

The implementation used the community python-a2a library. Its purpose was to make agent communication tangible through a small example that could be run and inspected, rather than hide every step inside a single prompt.
Separate discovery from orchestration

An Agent Card describes a service’s capabilities and connection information. A client still needs to decide which service to call, send an appropriate request, and handle the result. Publishing a card does not automatically create a reliable planning workflow.

The article also introduced task states and messages. These give the caller a way to represent work in progress, completion, failure, or a request for more input. The exact schema and discovery path belong to the protocol version used by the implementation.
Follow one trip request
The example’s coordinator queried the weather service, used the result to shape a search for indoor or outdoor activities, and sent the gathered information to the local model for summarization.

body.code:
Destination → weather agent
Weather context + destination → search agent
Weather + search results → local model → proposed itinerary

children.text: Weather and search used OpenWeather and Brave APIs. Those calls were remote; local summarization did not make the whole workflow offline. The weather endpoint also needs to match the question: current conditions cannot establish the forecast for a future holiday.
Make partial failure understandable

A useful planner should distinguish a missing weather response from a completed search with no relevant results. Preserve service errors and timestamps rather than letting the final model present incomplete data as a fully supported itinerary.

The historical weather example logged request details. When adapting it, redact credentials from URLs and logs. Authentication support in a protocol does not configure or secure the deployed services on its own.
Keep tools and agents in perspective

MCP and A2A address different integration boundaries: accessing exposed capabilities and communicating with agent services. Neither removes the application’s responsibility to coordinate work or validate results.
The author’s
tutorial code
preserves the example. Credit also belongs to
python-a2a
and its contributors. This is an edited account of the 2025 implementation, not a claim of conformance with a newer protocol release.

title: Local AI content pipelines: build a reviewable draft, then publish
excerpt: Use local models to structure research, drafting, and editing without confusing generated volume with useful technical content.

source.title: Local AI content pipelines: build a reviewable draft, then publish
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies. Removed promises of effortless income, zero cost, and automatic publication quality.

children.text: A useful content pipeline starts with a deliverable somebody needs: an API guide, a developer onboarding page, a lab exercise, or a clearer explanation of an internal system. Local models can help prepare those materials, but the value comes from their accuracy and usefulness.

The original article proposed a workflow using Ollama and CrewAI, with roles for research, writing, editing, and optional quality review. It also explored delivering the result as Markdown, HTML, or a document.
Define the input before assigning roles

For a technical guide, provide the relevant repository, documentation, supported versions, intended reader, and expected outcome. A writer supplied only with a topic has to fill far more gaps than one working from a specific source package.
Keep research notes and source links alongside the draft. An editor should be able to distinguish a documented fact from an assumption or a suggestion introduced during generation.
Give each stage a useful handoff

The researcher gathers relevant material. The planner turns that material into an outline. The writer develops the explanation. The editor improves clarity and consistency. A technical reviewer checks the instructions against the actual system.

body.code:
Source package → evidence notes → outline → draft
Draft → editorial review → technical verification → publication

children.text: More agents are not automatically better. Start with the fewest stages that make the work easier to inspect. Add a stage when it addresses a recurring problem, such as missing prerequisites or unsupported claims.
Understand the local tradeoff

Running inference locally can avoid a model API charge, but hardware, electricity, maintenance, and review time still have costs. Search tools and hosted integrations may also communicate outside the machine.

The original article described several possible commercial uses, including documentation services and educational material. These are potential delivery models, not evidence that generated content will earn revenue. A reader still needs a reason to trust and use the result.
Publish after the work is checked

For a tutorial, execute the commands in the environment it names. For an architecture explanation, compare the description with the implementation. For an onboarding guide, ask whether a new reader can reach the stated outcome without filling in undocumented steps.
The accompanying
book repository
includes the broader examples behind this workflow. The
Agents SDK edition
shows another way to coordinate a planner and writer. Choose the framework around the handoffs you need to observe and maintain.

title: MCP and REST APIs, part 1: expose warehouse operations as tools
excerpt: Build the service boundary first: FastAPI operations, Redis data, MCP tools, and direct inspection before adding a model.

source.title: MCP and REST APIs, part 1: expose warehouse operations as tools
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: An existing application already knows how to validate and perform its business operations. An MCP integration can expose selected operations to an AI application while keeping that service boundary in place.

The first part of this series built a small warehouse-order API with FastAPI and Redis, then connected it to an MCP server using fastapi-mcp. The exercise made it possible to compare a conventional API request with an invocation through an MCP client.
Start with operations you can test directly

The service created, retrieved, listed, updated, and deleted orders. Each order included an identifier, a customer name, items, and a status. Redis hashes held the order data, with a set tracking order identifiers and a counter supplying new IDs.

body.code:
POST   /orders             create an order
GET    /orders             list orders
GET    /orders/{order_id}  retrieve an order
PUT    /orders/{order_id}  update an order
DELETE /orders/{order_id}  delete an order

children.text: Test those operations through the API before adding a model. A tool wrapper cannot repair incorrect validation or an inconsistent data update. The storage example also needs an explicit persistence configuration if data must survive a Redis restart.
Expose a deliberate tool surface

The integration mapped API operations into MCP tools. This gives a client structured descriptions and inputs to work with; it does not make every generated argument valid or every available operation appropriate for every user.

In this example, the application layer is a useful place to retain business rules. That is a design choice for the warehouse service, not a claim that every database-backed MCP server must use a REST intermediary.
Inspect the MCP connection independently

The original walkthrough used MCP Inspector to list tools and invoke a read operation. That separates server connectivity from model behaviour. Compare the result with a direct request to the API before trying natural-language interaction.
The historical setup used SSE and an MCP endpoint mounted on the FastAPI application. Transport and mounting APIs vary by library version, so consult the
original project files
when studying that implementation.
Adding MCP does not supply authorization automatically. Decide who may read or modify an order at the service boundary. In
part 2
, the same tools are connected to a local model;
part 3
moves the workflow into a Python agent.

title: MCP and REST APIs, part 2: connect a local model to the service
excerpt: Connect Ollama and mcp-cli to the warehouse example, then separate tool discovery from correct execution.

source.title: MCP and REST APIs, part 2: connect a local model to the service
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: With the warehouse API and MCP server working, the next step is to place a local model in the loop. The second part of the series used Ollama and mcp-cli to translate natural-language requests into calls to the exposed tools.
The original experiment used a tool-capable model such as Qwen 2.5. Choosing a model that can chat is not enough to establish that it supports the tool-calling interface required by the client.
Verify discovery before interpretation

Start the API and its backing Redis instance. Configure the MCP client to reach the server, start local inference, and inspect the available tool list. In the historical client, the chat command /tools displayed those capabilities.

Then ask for all warehouse orders. Compare the returned records with a direct API query. Follow with a narrower request, such as listing orders in a pending state. These checks reveal whether the model selected a suitable tool and interpreted its result correctly.
Treat writes as a separate capability

The original demonstration also included deleting an order by customer name. A name can match more than one record, so a dependable application should resolve the intended order IDs before performing the operation.

For an illustrative cancellation flow, first retrieve candidate orders, display their identifiers and statuses, and obtain confirmation for the specific records to change. The service must still enforce the caller’s permissions. A persuasive natural-language request does not replace that boundary.
Understand the container network

The article packaged FastAPI and Redis in Docker Compose. Inside that Compose network, the application addressed Redis using its service hostname. A model server running on the host is a different connection and needs its own reachable address.

body.code: Local model ↔ MCP client ↔ MCP server / FastAPI ↔ Redis

children.text: Keep each connection independently testable. If the database is unavailable, inspect the API-to-Redis path. If no tools appear, inspect the MCP connection. If the wrong tool is chosen, examine the model interaction and tool descriptions.
The
original FastAPI files
and
mcp-cli project
document the historical setup. Local inference gives control over where model requests run; it does not by itself establish reliability or privacy for every connected component.
Continue to
part 3
to make this interaction an explicit Python workflow, or revisit the
service foundation

title: MCP and REST APIs, part 3: build an inspectable Python agent
excerpt: Use mcp-agent to connect tool discovery, local inference, and a warehouse summary without hiding the application’s responsibilities.

source.title: MCP and REST APIs, part 3: build an inspectable Python agent
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: The final part of the warehouse series moved from an interactive client to a Python workflow. It used the mcp-agent framework to connect to the MCP server, attach a local model, query inventory information, and summarize the result.
The earlier layers remained in place: FastAPI performed warehouse operations and Redis stored order data. The agent coordinated calls to that service rather than accessing the database directly.
Keep the runtime configuration visible

The historical configuration named the MCP server, configured its connection, and selected an OpenAI-compatible Ollama endpoint for inference. The example used Qwen 2.5 and a framework wrapper for the model interaction.

A server name in configuration is a reference the application uses to locate a connection. The MCP client discovers exposed tools through MCP. The FastAPI integration may derive those tools from API definitions, but the client is not independently discovering arbitrary REST endpoints.
Make the workflow observable

The example initialized an MCPApp, created an inventory agent, listed available tools, attached the model wrapper, and issued prompts. A follow-up prompt requested a summary of the gathered information.

body.code:
Initialize runtime → connect server → inspect tools
Attach model → request inventory data → inspect result → summarize

children.text: These are useful boundaries for logging and debugging. A model response should remain connected to the tool results that support it. Avoid logging credentials or unnecessary customer information while making those boundaries observable.
Decide what happens between runs

The original article proposed persistent memory as an extension. That raises concrete questions: which state belongs to a task, how long it should be retained, and whether a later run may rely on an earlier inventory snapshot.
A summary can become stale when orders change. Retained conversation history should not silently replace a fresh service query when the user asks for the current state.
Carry service rules into the agent workflow

Useful extensions include clearer tool descriptions, bounded retries, explicit handling of partial results, and authorization on the service. None is supplied merely by attaching a model or choosing an asynchronous runtime.
The
author’s agent example
and
mcp-agent project
preserve the implementation. Start with
part 1
for the API design and
part 2
for the interactive local-model connection. Together, the three layers show where each responsibility belongs and where a failure can be inspected.

title: Better AI agents show their work
excerpt: Why editable intermediate work can make an AI assistant easier to guide, verify, and improve.

source.title: Your AI Is a Caged Genius — Here’s How to Set It Free
source.editorialNote: Edited from Timur’s essay, first listed on QuickStart on 27 June 2025 and republished by Ardor on 12 July 2025. Condensed to its central design argument; unsupported statistics, speed promises, and absolute safety claims have been removed. MCP terminology has been corrected.

children.text: An assistant becomes easier to collaborate with when it exposes the work between a request and its answer. A query, a small script, or a visible set of source records gives the user something concrete to inspect and correct.

The original essay illustrated this with a project-status report assembled from several workplace tools. If the assistant selects the wrong channel or date range, a visible intermediate step lets the user identify the mistake before accepting the summary.
Make correction part of the interface

The design argument is straightforward: show which information was used and how it was transformed. Let the user revise an assumption and continue from that point. Treat example scenarios as illustrations, not measured productivity results.
Keep capability and control together

MCP means Model Context Protocol. It does not require a fixed linear workflow, and code execution can complement exposed tools. Neither approach removes the need for scoped permissions and review of consequential operations.

An isolated execution environment can reduce risk, but it cannot guarantee harmless behaviour. The useful goal is an assistant whose actions and intermediate results remain understandable enough for a person to guide and verify.

title: How the Claude Code team does code review: a short summary
excerpt: A short summary of Anthropic's engineering post on reviewing code at high volume: machines read first, people spend their time where risk is highest.

children.text: This is my summary of
How the Claude Code team does code review
, written by Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang and published on 15 October 2026. The ideas and numbers are theirs. Read the original for the full detail.
The problem

On the Claude Code team, Claude writes about 90% of the code. Between June and September, merged pull requests more than doubled. The share of PRs that needed a revert fell by over 40%. The team did not drop review. It moved most of the reading to machines, so that human time and attention go where they matter. The goal: merge most PRs with at most one person involved, with no rise in reverts or incidents.
Two jobs of review

The authors say review does two things: it catches problems before they ship, and it spreads understanding of the codebase across the team. Review now runs continuously. Usually Claude has reviewed and fixed a change before a person looks at it.
The layers
Before the PR:
Claude runs tests and builds. A subagent with fresh context reviews the diff.
On every PR:
required CI, plus an AI reviewer. Parallel agents look for bugs, and verifier agents vote on each finding. A security review can block the merge.
Human approval by risk:
a classifier puts each PR in a tier that needs zero, one, or two people. Sensitive paths always need a person.
Merge and release:
a merge queue re-runs the checks, changes ship behind flags, and rollback is fast.
Teaching the reviewer, and stopping loops

Reviewer guidance lives in CLAUDE.md and in a REVIEW.md file for each repo. Past incidents form an eval set that runs daily. Review loops needed work too. One PR went through more than fifty rounds, and about 59% of the flagged code was older than the PR. A three-round cap and diff-only re-review cut the share of PRs needing five or more rounds from 8.9% to 1.5%.
What people still do
Humans decide what to build, review risky code and architecture, and own the outcomes. The original ends with an adoption checklist: pre-PR checks, PR templates, risk tiers, and merge safeguards.

title: Building Braga in 3D at real scale
excerpt: How I built an interactive map of Braga where every building sits on its real footprint, and the rule that kept it honest.

children.text: I love Braga, a city in northern Portugal. I wanted a 3D map of it that felt like the real city. Not a toy. Not a diorama. A map where a church tower has the height of the church tower, and a street has the width of the street.

The project is a Three.js app built with Vite and plain JavaScript. The interface speaks Russian, English, and Portuguese. It runs at braga-3d.com. This is the story of how it got built, and what I learned about data on the way.
One rule: real scale only
Early on, the map had a diorama mode. It showed the city as a small, friendly model. It looked nice. It was also a lie, because the proportions bent to make things look good.
On 28 September I removed it. Real scale became the only mode. Models are authored one to one, in metres, on top of OpenStreetMap footprints.
A rule that you only believe is not a rule. So I wrote a check. The
check-fit
script fails if any model covers less than 97% of its OpenStreetMap extent, or falls short of its real height. If I draw a landmark too small, the build tells me.
I run other checks as well:
check-data
check-geo
check-dimensions
, and
count-tris
. Together they catch the quiet mistakes. A building that drifts by a few metres still looks fine to the eye. The checks do not look with eyes.
Where the data comes from
The ground is EU-DEM terrain. The city is about 17,000 buildings from OpenStreetMap. Walking routes come from OSRM. The pipeline lives in
scripts/fetch-*.mjs
and writes to
data/*.json
Three details cost me time. I list them so they cost you less.
First, the public Overpass servers are busy. The mirror that worked for me was maps.mail.ru.
Second, the main OSRM demo server ignores the foot profile. You ask for a walking route and get a driving route. The server at routing.openstreetmap.de does the job properly.

Third, panoramas. I wanted 360 views of the main sites. Wikimedia Commons has no equirectangular panoramas of Braga. The fallback is YouTube 360 video, and it covers 6 of my 16 sites. Detecting a 360 video needs a full Chrome user agent. The rule that works: the video metadata must show MESH or EQUIRECTANGULAR.
Working with agents
I built the first version on 28 September with a team of AI subagents. I did not let them all touch everything. I split the work by file ownership.

One group owned models, fit checks, and landmarks. One owned the scene, effects, and interface. One owned the data folder. Nobody edited a file that belonged to another group. This removed most of the merge trouble before it started.

Two habits saved me. Before each big round, I commit a work-in-progress checkpoint and make a snapshot tarball. Agent rounds sometimes stop halfway when usage limits hit. A checkpoint turns a mess into a clean restart.
I also keep one dev server on port 5173 and take screenshots with Playwright. The screenshots run on a software renderer, so they work on any machine.
Lessons
The hard constraint drove the architecture. "Real scale" shaped the footprints, the terrain, the checks, and the way the models are authored.
A rule needs a check.
check-fit
is what turns "real scale" from a wish into a build failure.
Notes about odd data sources earn their place. The working Overpass mirror and the OSRM foot-profile server are in my notes, so I do not rediscover them.
Braga was the first city. It would not be the last.

title: Cleaning 98 GB down to 21 GB, and the backup I chose not to make
excerpt: An audit of my Dev folder removed 77 GB. The more useful part was a plan I did not run.

children.text: In August I audited my
~/Dev
folder. It held 98 GB across 139 entries. After the cleanup it held 21 GB across 94 entries.
Most of the 77 GB was caches that rebuild themselves:
node_modules
, build output, package caches. Nothing exciting. The interesting parts were the decisions.
Scripts that start in dry-run mode

I wrote the cleanup as scripts: one to reclaim caches, one to remove redundant copies, one to back up risky repos, one to restructure. Each script does nothing by default. It prints what it would do. You pass a flag to make it act.
This habit costs a minute and prevents the worst mistakes.
A tree I did not build

I had a proposal for eight top-level folders: one for my company, one for products, one for skills, one for clients, one for experiments, and so on. The restructure script was ready. A dry run showed 120 moves.
I looked at the plan and called it questionable. I skipped it.
One fact limits any tree: two of my folders cannot move at all, because their paths are written into my tool configuration. The script stays in the toolbox, dry-run clean, in case I change my mind.

The index lives in my notes, not in the repo. For each project it holds a name, a purpose, and a status. Where I no longer remember the purpose, the entry shows a dash. I fill the gap when I next touch the project. I do not guess.
The backup I did not make
Some repos had history only on my machine. Some of them were work I did for an employer or for clients.

The first plan was simple: create private repositories on my personal GitHub account and push everything. It protects the history, and it is wrong. That code does not belong on a personal account. Moving it there is a policy decision, and the cleanup was not the place to make it.
I used
git bundle
instead. A bundle is a single file that holds a full repository history. It gives the same protection. Nothing is published anywhere.

An honest limit: the bundles sit on the same disk. That is not a real backup yet. A real one means a second location, and choosing it is still open. I would rather write that down than pretend the problem is solved.
One small macOS lesson
macOS is case-insensitive by default. I had a repo called
Skills
. A new folder called
skills
would have collided with it. If your restructure moves things between names that differ only in case, check this first.
Takeaways

Make destructive scripts dry-run by default. Treat a skipped plan as a result. Keep client and employer code out of personal accounts, and say so in the notes. Fill index gaps when you touch a project, not before.
A clean folder is nice. A folder whose rules you can explain is better.

title: Moving a small site off WordPress to a Cloudflare Worker
excerpt: A WordPress site became a static site on a Cloudflare Worker, with the same design and a mobile PageSpeed score of 93. What worked and what did not.

children.text: In October I moved a small professional site off WordPress. The old site ran on WordPress and Elementor. The new one is a static site served by a Cloudflare Worker. It went live on 19 October.
The owner gave me one hard rule: the design must stay pixel-identical. That rule shaped every decision.
The setup
The source is a folder with a
wrangler.jsonc
file and a
public
directory. One command deploys it:
npx wrangler deploy
. I used Workers static assets with an SPA fallback. Cloudflare Pages is the older route, and I did not need it.
A few limits showed up early. The
_redirects
file only supports 301 redirects. Workers assets do not support rewrites that return 200. Old WordPress URLs now redirect with plain 301s.

I also keep a plain-language set of diagrams for the owners: a system map, the update loop, and a "the site looks wrong" decision tree. A site is only maintainable if the person who owns it can read the manual.
Speed work, with measurements
I measured with real PageSpeed on 20 October. Mobile scored 93.
Here is what moved the score, and what did not.

Google Fonts load from a small script in the head, right after the first paint. Requesting them earlier cost about 25 points in the Lantern simulation. Self-hosting the fonts scored worse than the Google request in my tests. Deferring the main script also scored worse.
Images are WebP with a
srcset
. The
src
stays a JPEG for old browsers. The three.js code on the page is minified and loads lazily.
I tested each idea and kept only the ones that the numbers supported. Several ideas that sound right, like local fonts, were wrong here.
Two traps
First, caching. Files under
/assets
and
/vendor
are cached as immutable for a year. This is fast, and it has a catch: a changed file needs a new file name. Forgetting this means visitors see old files for a year.
Second, the page is rendered in the browser by a script. It loads React from
/vendor/react
and checks it against a hash. Cloudflare features that rewrite JavaScript, such as Rocket Loader, would break that check. I left them off.
The day the old site would not go away
After the DNS change, my own Mac kept showing the old site for a day. My home router had cached the old delegation. The site was live for everyone else.
The fix for testing is a direct request that skips the cache:
curl --resolve example.com:443:<worker-ip> https://example.com
A browser can lie about DNS for a day. A direct request cannot.
How I checked the design
"Pixel-identical" needs proof. I took before and after screenshots of all six routes at 390 pixels and at 1440 pixels. Then I compared them.
One gotcha: full-page screenshots leave lazy images blank. Scroll the page first, then capture.
Lessons

Measure before you tune. Keep a backup of the old public folder, and keep it out of the deploy. Write the manual for the owner on day one. And never trust one browser to tell you that DNS has changed.

title: One engine, many cities: what I learned scaling a 3D map
excerpt: Braga became four city maps on one engine. Notes on forks versus monorepos, performance work, and keeping long agent runs recoverable.

children.text: After Braga, I wanted more cities. I now have four real-scale maps that share one engine: Braga, Guimarães, Barcelos, and Porto. Porto is the flagship, with 70 places, at porto-3d.com. A fifth city is in progress.
Adding a city sounds like copying a folder. It is not. This post covers the decisions that mattered.
A repo per city, not a monorepo
On 30 September I had to choose. One monorepo with all cities, or one repo per city.
I chose one repo per city. Each is a template fork of
braga-3d
, named
<city>-3d
. A city has its own folder, its own deploy, and its own history.

The price is clear. A fix in the engine must be ported by hand to each fork. I see this with the flicker bug below: the fix has to be carried to each city by hand. The benefit is also clear. A mess in one city cannot break another city's deploy.
Each city is driven by a config file. A command runs the geodata pipeline for that city. Per-city models and texts live next to the shared engine. The engine does not need to know which city it runs.
Performance is a feature
On 10 October I spent a full day on Porto's speed. The draw calls dropped from 499 to 281.

The same round fixed a seam in the water, added a lite button on the loader for slow devices, and added roof art and 18 story illustrations. Streams that run in culverts no longer cut through streets. Six bridges over the Douro now land on raised pads instead of floating above the river bank.

One bug taught me a lesson about invisible geometry. A black square flickered on screen in one city. The cause was triangles with zero area. They draw nothing, but they confuse the renderer. The fix was small. Finding the cause was not.

I compared Braga and Porto on eleven axes. Porto led on eight. Braga led on three, among them live weather by default and the variety of its crowds. A comparison like this keeps me honest about what to port next.
Honesty about invented data

Some of my data is a guess. OpenStreetMap does not know how many storeys every building has. For buildings without that tag, my code uses a heuristic. The heuristic is invented. I decided to ship it and to record that it is a guess.
The same goes for translations. New language editions come from machine translation. They need a native speaker's review before I call them finished. I keep a status file so I do not forget.
Maps carry trust. I want to be clear about where the data is measured and where it is estimated.
Long runs need a recovery path
I build much of this with parallel AI subagents. They work in rounds. A round can die when a usage limit hits. This happened to me three times in two days, on 28 and 29 September.

So the handoff file matters as much as the code. It says what shipped, which commit is deployed, what is half done, and what is open. When I resume, I check the git status, finish or stash the cut-off edits, run
npm run verify
, and deploy once.
I commit before every big round. I snapshot before every big round. The cost is a few seconds. The benefit is that no agent can lose a day of work.
What is still open

The engine port to Barcelos and Guimarães is not done. Guimarães is the risky one, because its roads, water, and main files conflict with the new engine. Some art is not wired in yet. The Discover tab is missing in some cities. I would rather list these than hide them.
One engine, many cities works. It works because each piece has an owner, each rule has a check, and each run leaves a note for the next one.

title: Capturing UI inspiration with headless Playwright
excerpt: How I collect daily UI inspiration from product sites with a headless browser, and the small rules that keep the captures clean.

children.text: I keep a habit: each day I capture a few well-made product interfaces, so I can study how they handle layout, motion, and detail. On 29 October I ran it for five sites: Linear, Resend, Raycast, Cursor, and Framer.
This post is about the tooling, not the sites. The captures are for my own study. I do not republish them.
The tool I did not have

My capture workflow was written for the in-app browser of another coding tool. My Claude Code sessions do not have that browser. I could have stopped there. Instead I asked for a substitute: headless Playwright. I approved it, and the run went ahead.
The setup is small. I use
playwright-core
from the Playwright command-line package, with the headless Chromium shell that is already in its cache. Crops are made with
sharp
, which my site already uses. Frames and short videos come from
ffmpeg
The scripts live in a temporary folder. If the folder is gone, I rebuild them. They are not the valuable part. The rules are.
Rules that keep captures clean
Decline the cookie banner first. I click "Reject" before I capture anything. A banner in the corner of every screenshot is noise, and accepting it is not my choice to make for a study run.
Scroll in steps. A page that loads images lazily gives you blank boxes in a full-page screenshot. I scroll down in small steps and wait two seconds before each capture.

Accept that some things only draw on screen. One card on the Raycast page, the one called "AI Extensions", only renders while it is visible. I do not fight this. I write down which cards behave this way and move on. A note in the manifest is better than a hack in the script.
A checker for repeats
A daily habit has one risk: capturing the same site twice and calling it new. A small script guards against this. It compares each new bundle against the earlier manifests and flags duplicates.
The checker also gives me a rule for the next run. Rotate away from the five sites I just did. Each run gets a new dated folder in the same repository, with its own manifest.
A note on process
I keep the bundle in the repository of my own site, under
articles/
in a dated folder. Pushing to the main branch deploys the site, so I treat a push as a publishing step. I push the capture commits when I mean to.
One habit from this run is worth copying. When a tool I need is missing, I name the gap, pick a close substitute, say what I picked, and carry on. I do not wait for the perfect setup.
The loose end

The capture scripts live in a temporary folder, so I rebuild them from my notes when they disappear. The rules above are what survives. The duplicate checker is the one script that lives in the repository.

title: The cliff in the Crystal Palace garden: a bug that was not the terrain
excerpt: A grey cliff appeared in my 3D map of Porto. The terrain data looked guilty. It was innocent. The cause was a level pad cut 61.6 metres deep.

children.text: While building my 3D map of Porto, I sent my agents a screenshot. It showed a grey cliff wall where a garden should be. The garden belongs to the Palácio de Cristal, a landmark on a hill above the Douro river.
The map is at porto-3d.com. This post is about why that cliff was there, and why the first suspect was wrong.
The wrong suspect
The first suspect was the elevation data. The map uses a coarse elevation grid, and coarse grids make crude slopes. A cliff on a slope sounded like a data problem.
It was not. An agent traced the cliff to a different part of the pipeline. I call that part pads.

A pad is a flat platform. Real landmarks stand on level ground, but real hills are not level. So the engine levels the ground under each landmark. It cuts the hill where the ground is too high, and it fills where the ground is too low.
What the pad did

The Palácio de Cristal garden is large. Its pad was 417 by 438 metres. The garden outline falls about 88 metres towards the river. To make that whole area level, the engine cut 61.6 metres out of the hill. That is the pit, and the grey cliff was its wall.

The first fix capped the cut. That created a new problem. With a smaller cut, the pad could no longer reach the level it wanted from the hill side, so it filled in from the river side. It piled up 83 metres of ground on the shore of the Douro. A garden spur 80 metres high stood in the river.
So I had two bugs sharing one cause. The pad algorithm had no sense of proportion. It would move any amount of earth to keep a floor flat.
The caps
The fix gives every pad a budget.

A cut may not exceed one third of the building height, with a minimum of 3 metres. Gardens and streets may cut 6 metres. A stadium may cut 10 metres. A fill may raise the ground by 2.5 metres at most, and never at all below 1.5 metres above sea level. This stops pads from filling the river. Slope faces may not be steeper than 1 to 1.8.
Where a pad stands higher than the land beside it, the engine builds retaining walls under its edge. The final count is 429 wall segments. They cost 858 triangles and one draw call.
The Palácio extent also changed. The base now sits on the plateau, an area of 270 by 245 metres, not on the full garden outline.
The numbers
The worst cut fell from 61.6 metres to 10.8 metres. The worst fill fell from 83 metres to 11.2 metres.

The agent read the screenshots from before and after. The grey pit wall was gone. A grass plateau and street ribbons read sensibly. Two problems remained: a flat grey ring around the plateau, and bare lawn without trees.
A note on the terrain data

The terrain data was not the cause, but it is not perfect. I compared it against the EU-DEM source on six reference points. The mean error was 12.0 metres for the data I use, and 12.4 metres for EU-DEM. They are about equally accurate. Hill tops still read 10 to 30 metres too low. Serra do Pilar shows 70 metres, and the real value is about 100.
I wrote this limit into the notes. A map that states its own error is easier to trust.
Lessons
Do not blame the data first. Find the layer that changes the data. Here, that layer was the pad algorithm.
A fix can move a bug. Capping the cut made the fill worse. Check both sides of any change that balances two quantities.
Give every automatic correction a budget. An algorithm that can move any amount of earth will, sooner or later, move 61 metres of it.

title: Two deploy traps after a day of parallel agents
excerpt: Five agents worked on one repo for a day. The code was fine. Deploying it was the risky part, and a handoff file kept me safe.

children.text: On 10 October I ran several AI agents in parallel on my Porto map. Each one owned a set of files. One worked on the coastline, one on the sea shader, one on landmarks, one on terrain, and one on loading speed.
They did good work. The risky part came afterwards, when I had to put it all on the live site. I wrote a handoff file for the day I would resume. This post is about what that file warned me about.
Trap one: a commit that needs its neighbour
One commit changed the water code to import a new file,
coast.js
. That file did not exist at that commit. It only arrived in the next commit, from another agent.
Deploying the state between the two would break the build. The rule I wrote down: never deploy a state between the two commits. Deploy from the newest commit, after both are in.
This is a risk with parallel agents. Each agent commits its own files, and a commit from one agent can depend on a file that another agent has not committed yet.
Trap two: a build that edits its own inputs
The real build command runs a step before the build. That step rewrites
data/fits.json
, a file that records how models fit their real-world footprints. One agent knew this and built to a temporary folder to avoid it.
If you run the real build for a deploy, expect that file to change. Review the change before you ship it. A build that edits tracked files is easy to forget, and the diff is easy to miss.
A safe branch that was not safe
One agent produced a branch with lazy-loaded models and a lighter scene for weak devices. It passed all 15 of my verify checks. It looked ready to ship.
It was not. The branch left out the camera clamp, the boat models, the finer terrain, the pads, and the first wave of commits. Deploying it would have rolled back live work.
The agent's own deploy was also denied by the permission classifier, so nothing from that round reached the site. I wrote in the handoff: do not ship that branch. Deploy from
main
, after fixing the checks that fail.
Passing the checks told me the branch worked. It did not tell me the branch was complete.
What the light scene did
The lighter scene is worth a note. I measured it on a software renderer with the CPU slowed four times, as a stress test.
Time to ready fell from 58.1 seconds to 5.0 seconds. The mean frame time fell from 2742 to 45 milliseconds. Draw calls fell from 159 to 9. GPU memory fell from 349 MB to 6.4 MB.

These are test-bench numbers, not real devices. The handoff says so, and it lists the limits: no weather, people, vehicles, or trees in the light scene, and it is not yet the default for low-end devices. I need real-device numbers first.
What the handoff did

The handoff file listed each agent, what it finished, what it left half done, and which commits were local only. It named both traps. It gave the state of each repository and the live site. It also said which two verify checks were failing on
main
, so the first job on the next day was clear.
Agents can stop at any time, because of usage limits or errors. A handoff written before the stop turns a stop into a pause.
Lessons
Treat deploying as its own job. The code can be right while the deploy is wrong.
Do not trust a green check to mean "complete". Compare what a branch contains with what the live site already has.
Write the traps down. The next reader, including me, will not know them.

title: Giving Porto a real coastline
excerpt: The sea in my Porto map now follows the OpenStreetMap coastline, with moles, piers, lighthouses, and foam that follows the waves.

children.text: My Porto map is built at real scale, and the sea is part of the city. Porto's coast is not a simple line. The Douro meets the Atlantic among breakwaters, piers, and small harbours.
On 10 October the sea got a real shape. Two agents worked in parallel: one built the shore, and one built the look of the water.
The shore from OpenStreetMap

The new sea follows the real OSM coastline. It is a ring of 981 points. The sea mesh is a quadtree and costs about 5,000 triangles. Around it sit a shore apron of 22,600 triangles, 127 moles and breakwaters at 24,000 triangles, and rock armour on the moles at 44,000 triangles. The armour only appears for medium landmark classes and above. The map also has 79 piers and 17 lighthouses and harbour lights.
In total, the shore adds 96,800 triangles. The overview of the whole city stands at 1.94 million triangles.
The work comes with scripts: one fetches the coast data, and one checks it. A check that fails when the data is wrong matters more than the data itself. The same idea drives my fit checks.
One landmark, rebuilt
The mole at Felgueiras shows what real data does to a model. Its pin is now anchored to a real OSM node, 6 metres from the coast, at 41.14673 north and 8.6773 west.

The model is now the real OSM mole, rebuilt in 16 slabs, with a 10-metre hexagonal granite tower. The crown stands 4 metres above the root and 6 metres at the head. Those heights are my estimate, and the code says so.
Two other landmarks sit close to the new sea. Castelo do Queijo is 41 metres from the coast, and Praia dos Ingleses is 35 metres. The checks confirm that no landmark lies inside the new sea.
The look of the water

The second agent rewrote the water shader. Crest foam now comes from the Jacobian of the wave field, so foam appears where waves actually fold. Shoreline swash uses the distance to the shore. The swell no longer repeats, because its phase is warped. The Atlantic reads blue-green. The estuary reads olive, and the two blend at the river mouth.

The sea mesh carries three attributes for this: distance to the shore, depth, and a mouth mask. At the time of writing, the shader uses the shore distance and the mouth mask. The depth is stored but not yet used for shoaling.
A bug named after pixels

During this round we found a shadow artefact: a hatch pattern, like a screen door. The cause was small. The landmark focus effect, which fades buildings that block the view, kept one pixel in eight of each blocking landmark, in a 4 by 2 pattern. That pattern showed up in the shadows as a hatch. The fix drops the blocking landmark whole.
What is not done

I keep this list in the handoff, so I can keep it here too. The Leixões docks are not water in OpenStreetMap, so they are missing. Beaches have no foam line. The Passeio Alegre pools are not done. The rocks and apron have only one level of detail. Green strips still cross the sea at the river mouth. Four tower-like boxes stand beside the Congregados church, because OSM buildings sit inside its outline.
Real data is honest in both directions. It gives you the shape of the coast, and it shows you where the map still has gaps.

title: Making a 3D city run on a weak device, and where I fell short
excerpt: Lazy-loaded models and a lite scene cut memory and start-up time in my Porto map. Some goals stayed unmet, and I measured them honestly.

children.text: My Porto map holds 70 landmarks, a whole city of buildings, and a lot of art. On a good laptop it runs well. On a weak phone it can struggle. On 10 October I worked on two ideas to help: load models lazily, and add a lite scene for the weakest devices.
This post gives the numbers I measured. It also gives the goals I missed.
Lazy models

Models used to be built at start-up. Now each model is built in a worker, when the camera comes near. The model builders are split into 10 chunks. A queue caps how many models stay built, with a different cap for each performance class: 70 on the strongest, down to 8 on the weakest.
A script bakes the fit data for all models into one 56 KB file, and the build re-bakes it only when the inputs change. The check for this runs with the rest of my verify suite.

Results: - The critical chunk fell from 299.5 KB to 237.5 KB gzipped, a drop of 21 percent. - GPU memory fell from 672 MB to 543 MB on desktop, and from 335 MB to 214 MB on a high-end phone. - CPU-side vertex arrays for the largest class fell from 124 MB to 61 MB. - First frame and time to ready stayed the same, within noise. - V8 heap stayed the same, because typed arrays live outside it.
The lite scene
For the weakest devices, there is now a separate lite scene. It runs with
?scene=lite
, and the menu offers it as "Potato — lite scene". I measured it on a software renderer, with 1280 by 720 pixels and the CPU slowed four times.

- Time to ready fell from 58.1 s to 5.0 s. - Mean frame time fell from 2,742 ms to 45 ms, which is 22 to 36 frames per second. - The 95th percentile frame fell from 6,133 ms to 67 ms. - The overview fell from 0.88 million triangles to 0.126 million. - Draw calls fell from 159 to 9. - GPU memory fell from 349 MB to 6.4 MB, and heap from 178 MB to 18 MB.
On a simulated low phone with
?quality=potato
, time to ready fell from 38.3 s to 13.7 s, and it ran at 60 frames per second.
These come from a test bench. They are not real devices.
What I did not achieve

I did not make hitches near landmarks go away. Frames over 50 ms, when the camera approaches a landmark, were about the same before and after: 8, 6, and 10 before, and 8, 7, and 7 after, at four times CPU slowdown on the Low setting. The remaining hitches come from tile integration, clustered copies, and the first GPU upload.
I did not show the 1 ms phone slice that I aimed for.

The soak test fails. Over five minutes, GL memory grows past the gate by a hair on the Ultra setting, at 5.0 percent. It fails clearly on Low, at 14 percent. The working set of 70 models is larger than the Low cap of 14, so the map built 455 models and freed 403 in 300 seconds. The fix is to raise the Low cap or to stop freeing models near the camera.
The lite scene has limits

It has no weather, people, vehicles, or trees. Browsers with only WebGL 1 cannot run three.js r186, so those users see a message. The performance governor cannot switch scenes at run time. If it learns that a device is weak, the next visit starts in the lite scene. And the lite scene is not yet the default for the Low class, because I need real-device numbers first.
One more item is unverified. Gold pins lacked glow in the "after" overview shots. I suspect the governor turned effects off under load, not the lazy models. I have not confirmed it.
Lessons
Write the numbers that failed next to the ones that passed. A table with only wins is a poster.
Measure on a stress bench, and say that it is a bench. Real devices will disagree.
A lite mode is a safety net. It is not a reason to stop improving the full scene.

title: From Copilot to Colleague: the book and how I built it
excerpt: A ten-chapter book on AI engineering, built from 794 practitioner talks, where every claim points to the exact moment it came from.

source.title: From Copilot to Colleague
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from the book’s public README and method notes. Figures and claims come from those documents.

children.text: I built a book. It is called *From Copilot to Colleague: How AI Engineering Turns Models into Dependable Systems*. You can read it online at
fromcopilottocolleague.com

It is also a public experiment. The question was whether autonomous research loops, working from a real corpus, can produce a source-anchored book on AI engineering. The loops drafted the manuscript. The repository holds the method that produced it.
The book has one thesis. Models create possibility. Scaffolding creates trust. Organizations decide whether that trust compounds. The ten chapters are the argument for that line.
What the book covers

The book has ten chapters in four acts. The first act, chapters 1 and 2, states the problem. AI is moving from answering questions to doing delegated work, and cheap generation makes human judgment more visible, not less.

The second act, chapters 3 to 7, builds the scaffolding stack. It covers harnesses and specs that agents can use, evals as a control system, context as infrastructure, runtimes with a human control plane, and security and identity for systems that act.

The third act, chapter 8, is the stress test. Realtime voice removes the hiding places that text chat gives a weak system. The last act, chapters 9 and 10, widens the view. It asks what an AI-native organization looks like and which ideas endure when the tools change.
Where the material comes from
An AI-drafted book with no source of truth only remixes what the model already knows. I wanted a source of truth. The corpus is 794 talks from practitioners on the AI Engineer YouTube channel.

The rule of the project is simple: no anchor, no claim. Every claim in the manuscript carries a video, a start and end time, and a verbatim quote. The website shows these under each chapter, so a reader can jump to the exact moment in the talk.
How the quality is checked

No single model should grade prose shaped like its own output. A panel of three AI models from different families scores each chapter on six dimensions: humanness, voice, usefulness, evidence density, claim defensibility, and redundancy. The median score is the verdict. When the three models disagree by more than 20 points, that cell is flagged as the place to look.

The repository holds the whole method: the agent instructions, the research passes, and the judges. A bounded research loop takes one mission at a time, commits its result, and logs the pass. Every step is reversible and sits in git.
What I will post here

The book is the proof that the method works. The method is the deliverable. Over the next posts I will go through the book chapter by chapter. Each chapter gets three short posts: its core argument, a practical way to apply it this week, and one scene or example that teaches a single lesson.
Start where your own work hurts. If agents disappoint you, read about harnesses. If you cannot tell whether a change made things better, read about evals. If you ship to real users, read about trust.

From Copilot to Colleague

title: AI engineering starts when answers become delegated work
excerpt: Chapter 1 argues the hard problem in AI is no longer better answers. It is trusting a system that comes back with work done.

source.title: Chapter 1 — The Shift: From Assistant to Delegate
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 1 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A bad answer wastes a few minutes. A bad patch can stall a release. Chapter 1 of the book builds its whole argument on that gap.

For a while, the best thing AI could do was answer. It answered faster than search and more fluently than documentation. That changed user expectations and product design. It did not change the nature of work.

The change starts when the system must return with work done. Research this market and come back with a memo. Refactor this service, run the checks, and prepare the patch for review. The chapter says this is a different standard, and that most of AI engineering follows from it.
Work that looks finished

A helpful answer can be wrong and still useful. Delegated work costs more. It consumes time, touches systems, and shapes decisions. It also hides its mistakes inside output that looks plausible enough to pass a casual glance.

So the chapter says the main failure surface is not the work that looks broken. It is the work that looks finished. The same shape recurs wherever an agent reports on its own success: a test claimed to pass, a source claimed to be checked, a step claimed to be done. The review question changes. Stop asking whether the answer is good. Ask whether anything other than the system's own account can verify the work.
Three roles, one question
The chapter separates three kinds of system.
- An assistant suggests. - A copilot collaborates inside a tight human loop. - A delegate takes a unit of work and returns an artifact, a recommendation, or a completed step.

The labels matter less than where the human sits. With an assistant, nothing takes effect until you read it. A copilot lands its contribution inside a task already in motion, like a completed line of code you were already typing. A delegate steps you out of the moment-to-moment loop and back in at review. The work it produces changes the state of the world, and others rely on it.
Trust under action
Joel Hron describes the shift as a move "from helpfulness to productive." Once a system acts for users, prompt cleverness stops being the central problem. Trust under action takes its place.

The chapter defines AI engineering as the discipline of turning raw model capability into delegated work that can be structured, measured, supervised, and trusted. Prompting, retrieval, evals, workflow engines, guardrails, observability, and approval systems often look like separate subcultures. The book treats them as parts of one discipline. Each answers one question: what must surround intelligence before it is safe to delegate work to it?

The chapter also rejects autonomy maximalism. Maximum agency in every direction is not the goal. In many valuable systems, the right design is adjustable autonomy. Let the machine move quickly where risk is low and checks are strong. Slow it down where consequences are hard to reverse.
Try this

Pick one AI feature you run or plan to ship. Draw a line through its workflow and mark where the human sits: in the path of every step, beside the work, or out of the loop until review. Then find the last step before that human appears. Ask what proves the step happened, other than the system saying so. If nothing does, add a check there before you add any new capability.
This post draws on Chapter 1 of
From Copilot to Colleague

title: Five checks to run before you delegate work to an AI
excerpt: Turn the Chapter 1 checklist into a week of small, concrete steps that show whether your AI system is ready to take on delegated work.

source.title: Chapter 1 — The Shift: From Assistant to Delegate
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 1 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 1 ends with a checklist of five items. None needs new tooling. Here they become one task per weekday.
Monday: classify what you are building

Run the 24-hour test. Ask what happens if no human reads the output for a day. If nothing changes in the world, you have an assistant. If a pull request opens, a record updates, or a clock starts running, you have a delegate.
Write the answer next to the feature name. The label sets the rigor. The chapter says to treat a delegate with delegate-grade rigor, whatever the product page calls it.
Tuesday: test for dependability, not for a demo
Pick one task. Phrase the same request three different ways. Run all three with no one watching closely. Compare the results.

A demo has to clear the bar once. A production system has to clear it every time, unobserved. If the behavior drifts across the three runs, the system is not ready for delegation. The chapter says this holds no matter how good the single showcase run looked.
Wednesday: verify from outside

List every step where your only evidence is the agent saying it happened. Replace that evidence with something else: a test result you run yourself, a link to the actual source, a record in the system of record.

Rafael Levi at Bright Data explains why. Web-browsing agents that hit a block do not say so: "There's no error, no warning, just the wrong answer." The checklist states the rule in one line. If the only evidence a step happened is the agent saying so, you have no evidence.
Thursday: write the standard down
Ask a senior engineer for three conventions that live only in their head. Local naming rules, dependency habits, and rollback instincts are common examples. Put them in a file the agent can read.
The chapter's rule is that a standard must be made explicit before anyone delegates it, or the system will violate it silently. A model cannot inherit what the organization never wrote down.
Friday: name the missing piece
Walk through the seven things a trustworthy delegate needs:
1. the right context 2. usable tools 3. explicit constraints 4. evaluation loops 5. durable state 6. approval boundaries 7. observability

Mark each one present, partial, or missing for your system. Then name the one that is missing. The chapter asks you to do this before you blame the model for a failure. It says a missing layer is usually where the workflow fails first. A serious agent product with no trace view or approval queue has a reliability gap, not a leaner design.
What you hold by Friday
You hold a classification, a drift test result, a list of unverified claims, a standards file, and a named gap. That is a small plan, built from the evidence of your own system.

Short on time? Do Wednesday. Verification by something other than the system's own account is the habit that makes the other four useful. Open your agent's last report today and mark every claim you cannot check without asking the agent.

title: Meridian's coding agent worked until the scope grew
excerpt: A composite fintech case from Chapter 1 shows why erratic agent quality often points to the workplace, not the model.

source.title: Chapter 1 — The Shift: From Assistant to Delegate
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 1 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Meridian's coding agent felt magical on small tasks. Then the team widened the scope, and the quality turned erratic.

Meridian is a composite case in Chapter 1. It is drawn from real patterns, not from a single company. The chapter calls it the Software Factory, and the story returns in later chapters. Meridian is a mid-size fintech with an ordinary payments repository and a strong coding model.
The easy conclusion
Many teams reach for the same explanation at this point: the model is not good enough. They wait for a better one or switch to another.

The chapter pushes against that reflex. The model is not always the real problem. The deeper issue at Meridian is that nobody made the workplace legible enough for delegated machine work. A small task fits inside what the model can see. A larger task depends on things nobody wrote down.
What was hidden

Delegation exposes how much good work always depended on tacit human judgment. In software, that means local conventions, architecture taste, dependency discipline, rollback instinct, performance habits, and many non-functional expectations that senior engineers carry in their heads.

Strong teams absorb these so thoroughly that they mistake them for natural background competence. Then they hand the work to a machine, and the hidden standards turn into a liability. The system cannot reliably inherit what the organization never put into words.
What Meridian does about it

The team adds harnesses, specs, validation, context discipline, eval loops, runtime structure, and review surfaces. A harness is the structure around a coding agent that makes its work bounded and inspectable. As the team builds these, the repository changes character. It behaves less like a chat playground and more like a managed production environment for machine labor.

The chapter uses this case to show how quickly "AI coding" stops being a prompt problem and becomes a systems problem. Nothing in Meridian's story requires a smarter model. It requires a workplace that a delegate can read.
Run it on your own repo

When an agent does well on small tasks and erratically on larger ones, check the workplace before you check the model. Ask what a new colleague would need to know to do this work well. Ask whether any of it exists outside someone's head.

Try this exercise. Take the last task where the agent's output disappointed you. List the unwritten expectations the output violated. Each item is a candidate for a spec, a validation, or a repo rule. Write the first one into the repository today.

title: When code gets cheap, judgment gets expensive
excerpt: Chapter 2 argues that cheap generation does not remove the human contribution. It makes taste, the ability to tell good from convincing, easier to see.

source.title: Chapter 2 — Taste Still Matters When Code Gets Cheap
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 2 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A team can now generate ten versions of a feature instead of one. A founder can spin up a prototype in a weekend. A junior engineer can land patches that once took far longer. Routine output really has become cheaper.

Chapter 2 argues that cheap output does not mean cheap judgment. The bottleneck moves toward deciding what should exist, what quality looks like, which tradeoffs are acceptable, and what to reject. The human contribution does not disappear. It becomes easier to see.
Fundamentals were never about syntax

Matt Pocock says "software fundamentals matter now more than they actually ever have." That sounds backward. A capable coding system can fill in the syntax, scaffold the endpoint, and draft the tests.

The chapter answers that fundamentals are how you tell good output from merely convincing output. Which abstraction belongs here? Which dependency will quietly punish the team six months from now? Which draft only looks polished because nobody asked whether the premise is right? A machine cannot settle these questions for you.

These decisions always mattered. Their visibility changed. In a slower, human-only workflow, all production was expensive. Teams moved slower, touched fewer surfaces, and got incidental review inside the cost of making anything. Cheap generation strips away that natural throttle. A team can now pile far more work on top of weak decisions.
Taste is discrimination under abundance

The chapter defines taste as quality discrimination under abundance. It is the ability to notice the difference between output that merely works and output that fits. The tells are specific. A patch is technically correct but shaped wrong for the system around it. A component boundary is too clever. A naming choice will confuse the next person. A prototype convenience is about to become permanent structure. None of these trip a test.

Tuomas Artman, reflecting with Gergely Orosz on craft at Linear, asks: "What happens when agents are capable of doing everything immediately for you?" The obvious answer is speed. Artman's answer is sharper. When a small AI-equipped team can match your feature set, he sees tasteful, high-quality software as a way to keep some competitive advantage.
The chapter links this to architecture. The strongest engineers do more than clean up generated output. They shape the conditions under which good output is likely to appear in the first place.
An amplifier before a replacement

The chapter describes AI as an amplifier before it is a replacement. Good operators get more leverage. Sloppy operators get more slop, faster. A team with strong standards, explicit constraints, and people who discriminate well gets extraordinary speed. A team without them can industrialize confusion.

Once a machine can produce more work than a human can carefully inspect by default, taste becomes part of the operating system. The scarce skill is less often the manual act of producing. It is more often selecting, directing, constraining, sequencing, and refusing.
The chapter closes with a change of question. Many people ask what happens to programmers when code gets cheaper. A better question is what happens to standards.

Try it on your own team. Find one place where it accepted generated work because the work looked finished. Name the standard that would have told you whether it fit. If you cannot state that standard in one sentence, you have found the gap. Write the sentence down where the next reviewer and the next model can both read it.
