title: A week-long plan to keep taste in your AI workflow
excerpt: Five habits from the Chapter 2 checklist, laid out as steps a team can start this week to protect quality as generation gets cheap.

source.title: Chapter 2 — Taste Still Matters When Code Gets Cheap
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 2 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 2 ends with a checklist of five habits for anyone delegating work to a model. Each one fits into a single week. Here is how a team can start.
Run the framing gate before you delegate

Sean Grove at OpenAI says the new scarce skill is "writing specifications that fully capture the intent." The chapter turns this into a gate. Before you hand anything to a model, answer five questions in writing. What is the actual task? What counts as success? Which constraints are real? What may stay rough? What would make the result unacceptable even if it looks finished?
Treat the last question as the test. If you cannot answer it, you are not ready to delegate. With these questions unanswered, the chapter says, you do not have a task. You have a prompt.
Read every diff like its author
When you wrote every line, comprehension came free with authorship. A model breaks that bundle. It hands you working code you did not build, and you now pay for understanding separately.

So read the diff the way an author would. Reconstruct why each choice was made instead of confirming that the lines parse. Then trace one path the tests do not cover and ask whether the design survives it.
Sort your friction before you cut it

Armin Ronacher and Cristina Poncela Cubeiro argue in *The Friction Is Your Judgment* that some friction is judgment in disguise. The chapter gives a simple test. Cut a pause if removing it only costs keystrokes, such as boilerplate, glue, or scaffolding the model can regenerate on demand. Keep a pause if removing it costs a decision, such as whether the architecture can carry this change or whether the draft is right or merely plausible.
List your team's pauses on one page. Mark each as keystrokes or decisions. Protect the second group.
Know which mode you are in

Vibe coding is intuition-led building with low spec and high speed. The chapter calls it a mode, not a production philosophy. It suits discovery, where being wrong is cheap. Once someone who did not prompt an artifact into being has to maintain it, switch modes.
Add a line to your README or ticket template that names the mode. "Exploration" and "has to endure" are enough. The label turns the switch into a deliberate act.
Write your constraints down

Taste kept only in a senior engineer's head is easy to lose in delegation. Taste written into a harness, a spec, or a repo rule is harder to lose. Here, a harness is the structure around a coding agent that tells it how to work.

Start with the five rules your reviewers repeat most often. Write each as a sentence an agent could follow. The chapter says a team that states its standards explicitly can delegate more safely than one that relies on vibe and shared memory.
A check for Friday

The chapter offers one rule of thumb: when generation outruns review, the loop is not fast, it is unreviewed. Apply it at the end of the week. Compare what your team produced with what it read with care. If the first number is larger, give the habits above more room next week, and review before you generate more.

title: The Friday app and the Monday rewrite
excerpt: Corey Gallon's vibe-coding hangover, quoted in Chapter 2, shows when a fast exploratory build has outlived its usefulness.

source.title: Chapter 2 — Taste Still Matters When Code Gets Cheap
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 2 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: The app works on Friday. Corey Gallon at Rexmore calls what comes next the vibe-coding hangover. In his words, "then Monday rolls around, you want to add a feature… and you realize that you don't understand it, you can't maintain it, and you have to throw most or all of it away."
Chapter 2 quotes this scene because it holds a precise lesson about when speed stops paying.
The mode is fine

Vibe coding is low-spec, high-speed, intuition-led building steered by momentum rather than explicit structure. The chapter does not call it worthless. It says the mode can be brilliant. For exploration, interface sketching, rough prototypes, internal tooling, and one-off automation, it can be the correct move. It makes experimentation cheap enough that more people discover what is worth building.
The chapter's line is short. Vibe coding is not the enemy. Unexamined vibe coding is. A mode that works for discovery becomes a problem when it quietly hardens into a default production philosophy.
What Monday reveals

Look at what changes between Friday and Monday in Gallon's account. The app has not broken. It still works. What changed is the demand on it. It now has to change, and nobody understands it well enough to change it safely.

Nothing stood in the way of the build, and no test failed. The cost waited until someone needed the code to be maintainable. Chris Kelly at Augment Code makes the same point from the other side. AI code is still code, and vibes do not cut it in production. Production here means four-nines uptime, thousands of users, and gigabytes of data, where people who never saw the prompt pay for a mistake. The code still has to live somewhere. It still meets systems, constraints, users, security boundaries, and future maintainers. The machine does not repeal software reality.
One switch

The chapter reduces mode awareness to a single switch. Use vibe coding where the cost of being wrong is low and the goal is discovery. Leave it behind the moment the output has to endure. If Gallon's Monday is coming, the exploratory mode has already outlived its usefulness.

For genuinely disposable work, such as a one-off script or a prototype nobody inherits, the chapter says to skip the judgment overhead. The aim is not to slow every build down. The aim is to know which kind of build you are doing.
Try it before Monday

Pick one app or script built mostly by momentum. Ask whether someone who did not prompt it into being will have to change it next month. If the answer is yes, you are on the Friday side of Gallon's story. Write the spec you skipped. State the constraints. Read the code like its author would. Do it now, not on Monday.
For your next build, say aloud which mode it is. If it is exploration, set one review condition in advance: the moment someone other than the author has to maintain the result, the mode changes.

title: Blame the workplace before you blame the model
excerpt: When coding agents disappoint, the cause is often a repository nobody made legible. Chapter 3 argues the harness matters before the model does.

source.title: Chapter 3 — Harnesses, Specs, and Codebases Agents Can Actually Use
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 3 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: After a bad agent patch, the postmortem names a suspect: intelligence. The model missed a dependency. The model misread the architecture. The model broke a convention no outsider could have guessed.

Chapter 3 calls that diagnosis too flattering to the humans involved. Sometimes the model is not capable enough. But in production codebases, many failures point somewhere else. Nobody made the environment legible enough for delegated work.
The harness is the interface

Ryan Lopopolo puts the inversion bluntly: "The important thing is not the code but the prompt and the guardrails that got you there." Once a machine does implementation work, its surroundings become part of the product. The book calls those surroundings the harness. The harness is the repository, the specs, the validations, and the workflow. Together they decide what kind of work an agent can do.

Chat tools hide this. You type a request and wait for a patch, so the prompt looks like the whole interface. It is only the visible tip. The real interface is the codebase plus the setup instructions, naming conventions, tests, lint rules, examples of good patches, ADRs, and the performance or security rules that no single file states. A human engineer absorbs these slowly by asking teammates. An agent gets no apprenticeship unless the team builds one.
Slop is a missing standard

Good code carries many unstated decisions: tone, proportion, dependency choices, rollback safety, test shape. Lopopolo says one patch can require "500 little decisions" around underspecified non-functional requirements. The chapter says the exact number is not the point. The density is. A human fills those gaps with craft and context. An agent fills them by inference.

Lopopolo explains the mechanism. Models have seen "trillions of lines of code that make every possible choice of those non-functional requirements that you could ever imagine." Leave a requirement unspecified and the agent samples one of those choices. Nothing makes the sample yours.

So slop often does not mean a weak model. It means a task whose success criteria nobody wrote down. The rule underneath is hard: a standard that lives only in scattered memory is one the agent cannot inherit, and will therefore break.

That changes the prescription. Better prompting helps a little. Cutting the silent guesswork the environment demands helps more. Externalize architecture choices. Store examples of accepted patterns. Make non-functional constraints explicit. The chapter calls this harness engineering: the systematic conversion of tacit engineering judgment into durable, machine-usable constraints.
Who else benefits
A capable model in a murky repository resembles a strong engineer who joins a company with no onboarding and no record of past decisions. You may get lucky. You cannot count on it.

The benefit reaches past agents. New hires and future maintainers gain from the same legibility. The chapter says the agent only exposes the gap between the standards a team possesses and the standards it can operationalize.

Pick one standard your senior engineers enforce in review but have never written down. Put it where an agent can read it: a lint rule, a checked-in example, or a line in a spec. Then watch whether the next patch respects it. If it does, you have moved one piece of judgment out of a person's head and into the codebase.

title: Five repo changes that make agents useful this week
excerpt: A practical plan from Chapter 3. Five steps a team can start this week to turn a repository into a place where a coding agent can work.

source.title: Chapter 3 — Harnesses, Specs, and Codebases Agents Can Actually Use
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 3 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Clone your repo into a clean container. Time how long an agent takes to reach a green test run. That one test, from Chapter 3, shows how much of your setup lives only in people's heads.

The chapter says production software starts with the environment, not the model. The environment is the harness: repository, specs, validations, and workflow. Its checklist gives five steps a team can start this week.
Test the repo and fix the spec

First, run the fresh-container test. Every step that lives in someone's shell history is a hole. The agent will fill that hole by guessing. Write the step into a setup script. Run the test again until the agent gets there without help.

Second, watch for repeated hand-patching. If you keep fixing the same kind of mistake in the output, stop fixing the output. Al Harris says: "The spec then becomes the natural language representation of your system." Treat it that way. Find the line in the spec that under-specified the work, change it, and regenerate. Repeated correction signals that intent belongs in a persistent artifact the next run will read. Ask one question: would the intent survive a fresh agent picking up the task cold? If not, it does not belong only in the prompt.

Third, size the spec to the cost of being wrong. Not every ticket needs a design doc. Over-specification can turn exploration into bureaucracy. Save the ceremony for work that is large, parallelized, safety-sensitive, or expensive to review. Let everything else move fast.
Hold back the fan-out

Fourth, do not run many agents until one agent succeeds alone, nearly every time. Eno Reyes is explicit on this point. You cannot fan out parallel agents until single-task execution succeeds nearly 100 percent of the time. If you cannot tell automatically whether one change is safe, running twenty only multiplies unverified output. The validation you have sets the ceiling on how much you can delegate.

Reyes sets the bar low on purpose: "a slop test is better than no test." A rough check is a start. Once it exists, the next agent follows it, and the rules ratchet tighter. You can even ask a coding agent to find where your linters are not opinionated enough, then have it write the missing rule.
Audit the list and fix the first gap
Fifth, audit your repo against the agent-readiness list in the chapter. Check for these items:

- A stable folder structure. - Explicit setup, build, and run commands. - Type, lint, and test gates the agent can run repeatedly. - Architecture decisions stored in files. - Examples of accepted patterns for tests, APIs, migrations, and reviews. - Specs close enough to the work to survive handoff. - Narrow scripts for common operations.

Then fix the first item that is missing. Do not fix the easiest one. The chapter says each skipped item is a place where the agent will guess. The first gap you find is the first place a guess will hurt you.

None of this is glamorous. That is exactly why it matters. The chapter says the biggest gains in coding agents often come from removing avoidable ambiguity in the repository, not from clever prompting. Reyes puts a number on it: this is where "the real like 5x, 6x, 7x comes from," and "it's a choice that you as an organization have."
Start the fresh-container test on Monday. By Friday you will know which of your team's standards sit in files and which sit in heads.

title: A Tuesday in the slop era
excerpt: A migration passes every test and still breaks two rules nobody wrote down. A scene from Chapter 3 shows why the agent guessed.

source.title: Chapter 3 — Harnesses, Specs, and Codebases Agents Can Actually Use
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 3 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: The agent returned a migration diff in minutes. It compiled. Every test passed. It also broke two team rules, and neither rule lived anywhere the agent could read.

Chapter 3 tells this story through a fictional payments team called Meridian. They start where many teams start: a good model inside an ordinary repository. At first the results feel magical. Then the team widens the scope, and quality turns erratic. One Tuesday shows why.
The diff that looked clean
A senior engineer hands the agent a task: move three endpoints onto the new state machine, and keep the house style. The agent comes back with a clean-looking diff.
But the diff pulls in a parsing dependency the team had quietly banned. It also batches writes inside a loop. A payments incident taught the team to avoid exactly that pattern six months earlier.
The review does not save them. The reviewer catches the dependency, misses the write pattern, and approves. The convention resurfaces later, in a review comment nobody will search again.
The agent guessed

The team could say the model is inconsistent. The chapter says what they really mean is that the workplace is inconsistent. None of it was a hallucination. The agent guessed because the workplace gave it nothing firmer to stand on.

The scene shows a second failure too. The humans missed the same rule. The ban on the dependency was easy to remember. The write pattern lived only in the memory of an incident. A standard that exists only in scattered memory is one an agent cannot inherit, and one a reviewer can miss.
The unglamorous morning
The next morning the team does plain work. They check in an example of an accepted migration. They add a lint rule for the banned import. They write a setup script that ends the Slack archaeology.
Across the wider story, they also add agent-facing instructions and tighter lint and type gates. They stop relying on "everyone kind of knows how we do migrations here."

Nothing in that list needs a better model. The repo becomes less like a haunted archive of past decisions and more like a managed surface for machine labor. The chapter says the leverage sits where the team stopped treating its own tacit judgment as invisible infrastructure. It calls the larger pattern the software factory.
One lesson
When a passing diff breaks a rule, ask where that rule lived. If the answer is a person's memory or an old review comment, the agent never had a chance.
Take your last painful review comment. Ask where an agent would find that rule. If the answer is nowhere, turn it into a lint rule or a checked-in example before the next delegated task.

title: A working demo is not a control loop
excerpt: Models look right often enough that teams stop measuring. Chapter 4 argues that evals are the control system that makes delegated work safe to trust.

source.title: Chapter 4 — Evals Are the Control System
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 4 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A demo works twice in a row, and a team decides to ship. Chapter 4 of the book starts here, with a line from Ido Pesok that every team knows: “It worked first try... So from there we’re good to ship, right?”

The chapter names two failure modes. The first is obvious: AI systems can be wrong. The second is more dangerous: they can look right often enough that teams stop measuring. A prototype returns a plausible answer. A coding agent lands a decent patch in a familiar repo. Soon everyone speaks in the language of vibes.
The chapter does not call the demo fake. It says a successful demo is not yet a control loop.
What evals are for
The chapter says evals do not exist to decorate a launch deck or to compare two models in the abstract. They build a feedback system around delegated work.

Tasks have grown from single-line completion to repo-scale changes and multi-step workflows. As they grow, toy metrics drift away from operational reliability. The question changes. "Is the model smart?" gives way to "Can this system repeatedly do useful work in our environment without silently drifting out of bounds?"
So the chapter asks readers to drop the one-time gate and treat evals as an instrument panel. The panel shows four things:

- whether a new model is better on your work or only different - whether a prompt revision helped one slice and quietly hurt another - whether a new tool description raised completion rate but also raised latency or cost - whether the agent still handles the failures that hurt you last month
Without that loop, a team runs on hopeful anecdotes. It does not run a production system.
Reliability did not get easier

Some people talk as if stronger models dissolved the old reliability problem. The chapter disagrees. Samuel Colvin says, “We still want to build reliable scalable applications and that is still hard. Arguably it’s actually harder with Gen AI than it was before.”
Generative systems fail in a broader range of ways, including ways that look correct. Prompt design, retrieval, tool calling, context assembly, and business logic all interact.

That tangle makes a single score attractive. One number would shrink the uncertainty to a familiar size. The chapter rejects that shortcut and asks for a richer control system: representative tasks, credible scoring, production observability, regression sets from real failures, comparison loops, and a habit of turning mistakes into reusable tests.
The habit that matters

Once AI systems do work instead of suggesting it, measurement stops being optional. You cannot supervise every action. You cannot reason from benchmark scores to production trust, however impressive the model feels in a demo. Evals do not tell you whether your model is impressive. They tell you whether your system is safe to trust.

The chapter also calls "Do we have evals?" too small a question. A team can answer yes with one spreadsheet and one overworked engineer. The better question is whether the team has an operating habit that turns a real failure into a better system.

Take the last failure your AI system caused, even a small one that review let through. Write it as a test case with a clear pass condition. Store it where your team will run it again. That single case is the start of a control loop.

title: Build an eval habit from your own failures
excerpt: Five steps from Chapter 4 that a team can take this week to turn real failures into evals, traces, and a habit that keeps improving the system.

source.title: Chapter 4 — Evals Are the Control System
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 4 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Revert a fix from your own commit history, hand an agent the broken code, and see if it finds its way back. Chapter 4 of the book offers this recipe as the first of five steps. A control system sounds heavy, but each step fits in a week.
Start from real work

Step one: mine your evals from real failures. Naman Jain gives the rule: “Your task should be natural and sourced from the real world and then you should be able to reliably grade them.” His team crawls the commit history of real repositories and finds commits related to performance optimization.

Copy the recipe. Pick a fix that mattered in your history. Revert it. Give the agent the broken state. Score whether it returns to the known-good commit. The chapter says this beats a benchmark built in a conference room.

Seed the early set by hand. Samuel Colvin describes the common practice: people have “some subset of data that’s been like human annotated.” Humans know which failures are expensive. If a class of mistake bit the team three times last month, it belongs in the test set.

Step two: grade the path, not only the destination. Two runs can land on the same diff. One took a safe route. The other deleted a failing test to turn red into green. A check on the final files passes both. Score whether the agent reached the known-good end state, and inspect how it got there.
Weight and trace

Step three: weight slices by consequence, not frequency. Application evals mix objective checks with human review and carry slice-level metrics. The slices are not equally important, so one averaged score hides the failures that cost the most. Let a rare, expensive failure outweigh a common, trivial one. Ask whether the output was correct, usable, safe, timely, and cheap enough for this workflow.

Step four: instrument every production run as a trace before you think you need it. A trace you never captured is a regression case you can never recover. Arize’s Dat Ngo puts it this way: “code doesn’t audit agents or harnesses — it’s actually the telemetry that does that.” Phil Hetzel says observability and evals are the same problem from a systems perspective. Production traces feed the next offline eval set. A failed coding task becomes a benchmark slice. A costly retrieval miss becomes a dataset item.
Ask the habit question
Step five: swap the inventory question for the habit question. "Do we have evals?" is too small. Ask whether your team has a habit that turns this month's failure into next month's regression test.

That habit needs owners. Someone owns the datasets. Someone decides how failures are labeled. Someone adjudicates when an automatic judge disagrees with expert review. In immature teams, one careful engineer and one spreadsheet carry all of this. The chapter calls that a reasonable beginning and not a durable end state.
Here is a plan for the week.

- **Monday:** pick one painful failure from your history and write it as a case. - **Tuesday:** decide how you will grade the path as well as the result. - **Wednesday:** name the one slice that costs you most when it fails. - **Thursday:** confirm that production runs leave traces you can replay. - **Friday:** name an owner for the dataset.
You will not finish a mature eval program in five days. You will have a seed, an owner, and a loop. Start with Monday's case today.

title: The patch that looked fine and stalled the backfills
excerpt: A rate-limiting patch compiles, passes tests, and still drifts production. A scene from Chapter 4 shows what a regression case is for.

source.title: Chapter 4 — Evals Are the Control System
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 4 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: The patch compiled. The tests passed. The pull request description was tidy. Two days after it merged, admin backfills began to stall. Chapter 4 of the book uses this scene to show what evals are for.
The scene follows Meridian, the fictional payments team from the previous chapter. The team has moved from small safe edits to multi-file implementation tasks.
A tidy pull request
The agent gets a task. Add rate limiting to an internal API endpoint, thread the new behavior through a background job, and preserve an existing admin override.
On first inspection the run looks good. A reviewer glances at the diff and says what the chapter calls the most expensive sentence in modern engineering: looks fine.

Two days later support reports something odd. A class of admin-triggered backfills is stalling in production. Nothing is fully broken. Jobs queue longer than usual. Customers are not yet furious and engineers are not yet panicking. The system is drifting into a worse state.
What the postmortem found
The agent did implement rate limiting. It even mirrored the main service pattern correctly. But it also applied the same throttle to the backfill path, where the intended rule was different.

That exception lived in two places: an old review comment and the head of Meridian's most senior payments engineer. The code still type-checked. The unit tests still passed, because none covered the override path under production-like volume. The patch was locally plausible and globally wrong.

The chapter says this is the shape of many AI failures in production. They are not spectacular hallucinations. They are near-misses that survive ordinary review because each move looks reasonable. The model did not go insane. The system had no reliable way to notice that an important slice of behavior had regressed.

The scene also answers a common hope. Colvin says a coding agent can use type checking “to basically mark its own homework.” Static checks, tests, and schemas catch the errors a machine can already define. This patch cleared every one of those gates. Self-verification cannot certify that the whole change was correct. Production reliability needs several layers of evidence.
From lesson to instrument
Once Meridian sees the pattern, the eval work almost writes itself.

- The team adds a regression case for the admin override path. They later call it the admin-override regression. - They mine earlier incidents for similar special-path behavior. - They create a task slice for patches that touch both product logic and operations logic. - They stop asking only whether a patch passes. They ask which real failure families it still protects against.

The chapter calls this a control system in practice. It converts an expensive lesson into a reusable instrument. Notice what moved. The knowledge lived in an old comment and in one senior engineer's memory. Now it lives in a test that runs every time, whoever is on call and whichever model wrote the patch.

After your next incident, do not stop at the fix. Ask who held the knowledge that would have prevented it. Write that knowledge as a case that fails when the behavior regresses. If the answer is one person's memory, you have found your next eval.

title: Context is the working set, not the knowledge base
excerpt: Chapter 5 says AI systems fail when they hand the model the wrong working set, not only when the model is weak. A stronger model makes bad context cost more.

source.title: Chapter 5 — Context Is Infrastructure
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 5 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A company can hold millions of documents and still show its AI the wrong three paragraphs. Chapter 5 of the book starts here. Useful AI systems do not fail only because the model is weak. They fail because the system cannot assemble the right working set of information at the right moment, in the right shape, at a cost the product can bear.
Access is not context

The chapter says one confusion persists in AI product work: the belief that access to more information equals better context. It does not. A codebase may hold thousands of files. A legal system may hold a vast corpus of precedent. None of that guarantees the model sees the right few things for this task, in this turn, under this deadline.

The chapter names the usual sequence. The team says the system can reach the knowledge. The product disappoints. The team blames the model. Often the system simply handed the model the wrong working set: too much, too little, or the right ingredients in the wrong order.
So the chapter replaces one question with another. Do not ask what the model can access in principle. Ask what the model should be looking at right now to do this job well.
A bigger window is not memory
The chapter cites Jack Morris on this point: stuffing context is not memory, updating weights is. Shoving more tokens into the window, the chapter says, is closer to panic than architecture.

The chapter also warns against using retrieval as a universal substitute for state, history, and durable understanding. Working memory, session history, and long-term memory are different layers. Each has its own update rules, its own freshness needs, and its own failure modes. Some things should stay out of the window until someone reintroduces them. Every carried-forward item costs tokens, competes for attention, and may quietly mislead the next step.
Misassembly is not hallucination

Teams often call a bad answer a hallucination. Sometimes it is. Just as often, the chapter says, it is context misassembly. The remedy differs. Hallucination invites better model behavior. Misassembly invites better infrastructure.
A stronger model raises the stakes

Some readers expect context work to fade as models improve. The chapter argues the opposite. A stronger model raises both the return on good context and the cost of bad context. It does more with the right evidence in front of it. It also generates more persuasive nonsense when the context is badly assembled. A better model is a reason to invest more in context, not less.

For that reason, the chapter puts context in the same bucket as harnesses, evals, runtimes, and security. These are engineered surroundings. They decide whether intelligence becomes useful. The chapter's image for the goal is a working binder. A strong professional does not walk into a meeting with every file the firm has ever touched. They bring the current notes, a few precedents, and a clear sense of what governs. A machine colleague does not need infinite information. It needs the right binder.
Try this

Take the last answer your assistant got wrong. Write down every item the system put in front of the model for that turn. Then mark which items the answer needed, which items it did not, and which governing item never arrived. If the governing item never arrived, the model was not the problem. Fix the assembly first.

title: A week of context checks for your retrieval system
excerpt: Five checks from the Chapter 5 checklist, one per working day, to learn whether context assembly or the model is your real problem.

source.title: Chapter 5 — Context Is Infrastructure
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 5 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 5 ends with a checklist of five items. Each fits in one working day. Run them Monday to Friday and a team learns whether its context system helps the work or only looks good in a diagram.
Monday: plot accuracy against document count

Take your retrieval system and vary the number of retrieved documents. Plot accuracy for each count. If accuracy drops as you add documents, the middle of the context window is getting lost. The chapter says this is not the model getting dumber. Its fix is better assembly, such as summarization, graphs, or iterative retrieval, not a bigger window.
Tuesday: measure how little the answer needed

Most teams track how big the index is. The chapter asks teams to track how little of it the answer needed. Kuba Rogut relays Jeff Dean on the sizing rule: you do not need a trillion tokens at once, you need the right million. So record how much of what you retrieved each task actually used.

The chapter adds a cost figure. Rajkumar Sakthivel's team at Tesco states that 90 percent of AI cost is input: files, search results, and context you send in. Retrieving only the relevant slices of a codebase, instead of pasting whole files, cut their input tokens by 94 percent on a public benchmark. He says this is a best case, and real setups will not match it. Use it as a reason to measure, not as a target.
Wednesday: match the mechanism to the answer

Match each retrieval mechanism to the shape of the answer. Use vector search when the answer is a single similar passage. Use graph traversal when the answer is a path along explicit relationships. Use keyword or metadata filters when exactness matters. Do not make one mechanism carry all three jobs. Mature systems layer them.
Thursday: split the eval in two

Score retrieval and generation as separate questions. First check whether the governing passage reached the assembled working set at all. That is a recall measure on the context layer. Only then score whether the model used it correctly. If you score only the final answer, a context-assembly bug looks exactly like a model getting dumber. Then a model upgrade gets wasted on a retrieval problem.
Friday: change one default

The last item concerns people. When a fix depends on users opting in, assume almost no one will. The chapter tells the GitHub story. Community contributions pushed its remote MCP server past a hundred tools, and the agents got measurably worse. The first fixes were opt-in tool sets and dynamic discovery. Almost no one used them, because most users never touch the JSON config. GitHub changed the default and cut the initial tool-load context by 49 percent. The number of tools the agent could call did not fall. The number it had to read did.
So on Friday, find one setting in your system that nobody changes. Change its default.
Close the week with one page

Write four lines. How accuracy moves with document count. How much context a task really uses. Whether the governing passage arrives. Which default you changed. Pin the page where the team sees it. The weakest line is your first fix.

title: The deduction that cited the wrong source
excerpt: A tax assistant at Hargrove ranked a public explainer above a senior attorney's matter note. The fix taught the team what context topology means.

source.title: Chapter 5 — Context Is Infrastructure
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 5 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A tax associate at Hargrove asks the firm's assistant to trace the support for a deduction a client has claimed for years. The assistant answers fluently. It cites a clean-looking authority, and the answer reads as decisive. It is also wrong for this client.

The chapter follows this scene from Hargrove's early build-out. The firm's tax practice runs an assistant that began as a helpful chat surface. It summarizes documents, answers questions, and cites plausible authorities. Users like it. Then they ask for more. They want the assistant to do the work, not only to help them think.
What went wrong

The cited authority was a public explainer whose wording matched the query almost perfectly. The governing position lived elsewhere. A senior attorney had written it earlier in a matter note, in a different file, under a jurisdiction the explainer never mentioned.

The system ranked the explainer first because nothing told it that a public article and a matter-specific note are different kinds of evidence. The model did not invent a source. The explainer was real. The system treated all text as interchangeable.
The chapter says simplistic retrieval systems flatten everything into one big searchable pile. They act as if the only problem were semantic similarity.
The remedy
The chapter states it plainly: the remedy is not a smarter model. The team types its knowledge topology into the system. That means three changes.

- Source typing ranks internal precedent above public background. - Access boundaries apply per matter. - The retrieval surface carries provenance, so the associate can see which layer an answer came from.

The chapter calls this idea context topology. Different kinds of information are not interchangeable text. A draft contract is not signed language. An old Slack discussion is not a policy. A matter note from a senior attorney is not a general explainer from a public source. Usefulness depends on what kind of thing a document is, how it relates to other documents, how trustworthy it is, and how recent it is.

The chapter then draws the stakes. In high-stakes work, a system that is 90 percent right for unclear reasons can still be professionally unusable. The associate needs to see why an answer is right. Provenance shows it.
The chapter closes the scene with a line worth keeping: the misranked matter note becomes the scar the rest of the build-out is designed around.
Do this today

List the kinds of documents your assistant can retrieve. Take each pair and ask whether one kind should outrank the other. Where the answer is yes, write the rule into the system. Then show the source type next to every citation your assistant gives.

title: Agents are stateful workflows with probabilistic nodes
excerpt: Chapter 6 says a production agent needs durable state, recovery, and human review points. A chat transcript supplies none of them.

source.title: Chapter 6 — Runtimes, State, and the Human Control Plane
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 6 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A chatbot can get away with amnesia. A production agent cannot. Chapter 6 of From Copilot to Colleague opens with those two sentences and spends the rest of the chapter on what follows from them.

A chat system answers a question, emits a patch, or suggests a draft, and then it is done. Work that runs across time, tools, failures, and approvals is different. The chapter says the question stops being whether the model can produce a smart next token. It becomes whether the surrounding system can keep intent, survive interruption, recover from error, show its progress, and stop in the right places for human review.
A transcript is not state

The chapter says many impressive demos break here. The model is good enough and the context is strong. But the builders made the system like a conversation when it needed to be a workflow. It loses track of what already happened. A retry repeats work or performs the same action twice. An approval arrives after the risky step. The agent does not fail because it is unintelligent. It fails because it has nowhere durable to stand.

A transcript cannot be that place. It does not cleanly show task progress, pending approvals, completed tool calls, or which intermediate outputs are binding and which are disposable. Samuel Colvin marks the break point: "Once we get into longer running workflows, that's where it really becomes a problem." A short answer can be regenerated. A half-finished multi-step legal workflow cannot.

Preeti Somal supplies the chapter's backbone. She says that at the core of agentic AI applications is a complicated workflow that needs to handle state potentially over long periods of time, with human interaction for approvals. The chapter condenses this into one sentence: useful agentic systems are stateful workflows with probabilistic decision nodes.
Structure makes agency survivable

The chapter calls the common debate a category error. People say workflows are rigid and agents are flexible, so choosing a workflow means giving up agency. The chapter reports the opposite lesson from production systems: workflow structure is what makes useful agency survivable.
The framing explains why pause and resume matter. It explains why retries should not live in ad hoc prompt logic, and why approvals belong inside execution.
State, in this view, is a structured memory of work. For a coding task it holds the current plan, completed tool runs, validation status, and pending questions for the reviewer.
The human control plane

The chapter's title concept is the human control plane. It is the set of interfaces, approvals, visibility layers, and intervention mechanisms through which people supervise delegated machine work. The chapter treats it as an architectural layer. It does not treat it as a crutch on the way to full autonomy.

A chat transcript is usually too thin for supervision. Operators need queue views, roll-up summaries, pending-review surfaces, and clean points to step in. If the only way to supervise an agent is to read back through thousands of tokens, the control plane does not exist yet. Eric Zakariasson puts the need in plain English: "Here's what everyone is working on... and here's what you as a human need to review."
Control does not mean a person approves every step. The chapter calls it a gradient. The design task is to place the few checkpoints that carry the most judgment.
Try this today

Pick one agent workflow your team runs. Write down what it must remember if it stops halfway: the plan, the finished tool calls, the pending questions for a human. Then check where that list lives. If it lives only in the prompt window, you have a chat and no runtime. Move the list into stored state first. Decide where a person steps in second.

title: Runtime decisions to settle before you add more agents
excerpt: Chapter 6 ends with five runtime checklist items. Here they become steps for this week, from replay versus snapshots to isolated environments per worker.

source.title: Chapter 6 — Runtimes, State, and the Human Control Plane
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 6 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Add no new agent until you can fill one page with five decisions. Chapter 6 of From Copilot to Colleague closes with a five-item checklist on agent runtimes. This post turns each item into a step for this week. Take them in order, because each one shapes the next.
Decide how the system continues

First, choose replay or snapshots on purpose. A replay design keeps an event history and rebuilds state from what happened. The chapter says to reach for it when causality and auditability are the point, so state emerges from recorded steps and not from opaque frozen blobs. A snapshot design saves checkpoints of working state. Reach for it when fast continuation and elaborate live state dominate, so pause and resume stay cheap.

This week, hold a short meeting and finish one sentence that says whether the system needs replay or snapshots, and why. If nobody can finish it, the team is not ready to build either. The chapter notes that at this point teams make the decisions mature distributed systems always make: what gets persisted, what gets recomputed, and what must be auditable.

Second, place checkpoints where judgment lives. The chapter says the design question is not how to keep a human in every loop. It is where the few checkpoints that carry the most judgment should sit: before, during, or after execution. Its coding example lets subagents explore, draft, and run validations alone. Merge decisions, large architectural changes, and dependency additions wait for review. Mark those on your workflow diagram and remove approvals everywhere else.
Decide how the system spends and isolates

Third, route each step to the cheapest model that still passes the eval, and no cheaper. The chapter calls the choice of model a control-plane decision made per task, not a global default set once. Laurie Voss at Arize says to use cheap models for simple queries and expensive models in your agent for complex ones. Routing adds a failure surface, though. A misroute hands a hard task to a cheap model that quietly botches it. Run your eval on the cheaper route first, and keep verification in place behind it.

Fourth, give every parallel worker its own isolated, ephemeral environment. Workers that share one dev setup collide on the same branch, ports, and database. One agent's migration breaks the others mid-run. The chapter says a git worktree suffices for trusted edits and untrusted, side-effecting work wants a VM. Rene Brandel at Casco warns that "if you just use containers ... that's not an isolation layer," because agent code can get root and move laterally. List how each worker is isolated today and mark which ones run untrusted work.
Decide who sees what

Fifth, design observability for two audiences. Engineers need deep inspection of one trajectory. Operators need roll-up supervision across many. Good traces capture plans, tool calls, state changes, intermediate outputs, timings, and the boundaries between durable steps. Build redaction and risk-based views in from the start. The chapter warns that richer traces buy trust and retention risk in the same breath.
The page
By Friday the page holds five short lines:
- Replay or snapshots, and why. - Where humans review. - Which model runs which step. - How each worker is isolated. - Who sees which trace.
If a line is blank, fix that line before you add a worker. More workers multiply whatever the runtime already lacks.

title: When Meridian's subagents disagreed
excerpt: In Chapter 6, Meridian asks its agents to investigate, patch, and report. Parallel work turns into fragments, and coordination is the missing piece.

source.title: Chapter 6 — Runtimes, State, and the Human Control Plane
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 6 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: One subagent finds the failing code. Another, working from a slightly older view of the branch, proposes a different patch. That is the scene Chapter 6 of From Copilot to Colleague uses to show what parallel agents break.

The chapter's case study is Meridian, a team running what the book calls a Software Factory: a repo and a quality system prepared so that agents can do real engineering work. By this chapter, Meridian has rebuilt its repo. It has added eval slices that catch special-path mistakes. Small delegated work goes well.

Then the team raises its ambition. Instead of isolated patches, it asks the system to investigate a bug, spawn a few subagents, inspect a cluster of files, propose a fix, run checks, and prepare a reviewable summary for a human.
What went wrong
The two patches collide. A retry of the validation step reruns something the first attempt had already completed. The human reviewer receives fragments of work, not a coherent roll-up.

The chapter compares the result to a workshop full of talented workers without a foreman's board, without station history, and without a clean shift handoff. The system still has intelligence and context. It has no stable execution semantics.

Look at what did not fail. The model was fine. The workers were competent. The failure sat in the space between them. More workers mean more intermediate artifacts, more duplicated effort, and more state to coordinate. The chapter puts it bluntly: parallelism without recomposition is just chaos at higher speed. The design challenge is not how to spawn more workers. It is how to merge, compare, inspect, and route their outputs so the human stays oriented.
What the chapter offers

Independence must come from the environment, not from the task split alone. Each worker needs its own isolated, ephemeral environment. Without one, a single agent's migration breaks the others mid-run.

Lou Bichard at Ona names the missing piece. He argues the runtime is solved, with "many options for this now, sandboxes and containers", and so are triggers and orchestration. "The thing that's missing," he says, "is coordination." He means an agent-native primitive that lets parallel workers pick up tasks, signal completion, and hand off without a human stitching them together. His candidate building blocks are "state machines, by building out workflows."

The chapter adds that teams shipping production multi-agent systems have not agreed on an answer. Each substitutes a known mechanism for the missing one. Factory runs features serially with one active writer. Anthropic's long-running agents write a contract to files on disk before any code is produced. Others use state machines with durable execution. That makes three substitutes for one primitive that does not yet exist.
The lesson
Before a team adds its fourth subagent, it should answer three questions.
- Which worker owns each task? - Where is the shared record of what is done, so a retry does not repeat finished work? - Where does the human see one roll-up instead of fragments?
If any answer is missing, run the work serially with one writer until it exists. That is slower. It also removes the coordination problem by construction.

title: Build so that an agent being wrong is survivable
excerpt: Chapter 7 says a model can never enforce its own power. Build sandboxes, narrow scopes, and boundaries that hold when the model is wrong.

source.title: Chapter 7 — Security, Identity, and High-Stakes Trust
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 7 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A helpful model can get away with being vague about power. An acting system cannot. Chapter 7 opens with those two sentences and spends the rest of the chapter on them.

An agent that reads across accounts, calls tools, executes code, or keeps working after the user looks away changes the trust question. Trust stops being a judgment about how smart the model sounds. It becomes an architecture question. Who is this system acting as? What can it reach? What can it do without asking again? What evidence remains afterward? How fast can its power be reduced or revoked?
The model is not the enforcement layer
The chapter gives one rule: a model can never be the final enforcement layer for its own power.

Take an agent that can execute code, browse untrusted content, open files, or chain across tools. The design must assume someone can push it into bad behavior. A malicious instruction can do it. So can a poisoned page, a bug in a tool description, or a plain misunderstanding. The cause matters less than the consequence.

The chapter's blunt principle follows. Assume the agent will sometimes be wrong, and build so that being wrong is survivable. In classic software, developers wrote the code paths and could know them ahead of time. In agentic software, the system picks among many paths at runtime. The model may improvise. The environment should fail closed.
A code agent shows the stakes

The chapter uses the Software Factory to make this concrete. A code agent with repository access is dangerous when it writes a bad patch. It is also dangerous when it can quietly inspect secrets, change CI configuration, add a dependency, call external services, or keep iterating after a misleading instruction entered the loop. Once code execution is in play, the idea that a better prompt solves trust is hard to defend.

So the chapter moves the conversation to runtime design: operating system boundaries, execution isolation, token scope, credential lifetimes, and mediation layers. These decide what the system can do when the model is confused, manipulated, or simply too eager.

The chapter does not argue against alignment work. A serious discipline studies what a model is disposed to do, refuse, and value. The book covers a different layer: the boundaries, identities, sandboxes, and audit trails that must hold even when the model's inner alignment is imperfect.
Narrow power helps twice

Narrow powers protect the organization. They also shrink the number of tempting but unsafe paths the model can wander into. A tighter design often makes the system easier to reason about, not only safer.
The chapter sums it up in one sentence: safe delegation comes from making carelessness less powerful, not from asking the model to be careful.
One thing to do

Pick one agent you run today. Find the step where it holds the most power. Write down the worst plausible mistake there, whether from a bad instruction or a plain error. Then ask: would that mistake be survivable?
If the answer is no, narrow the power at that step before you spend another hour improving the prompt.

title: Five agent security steps a team can take this week
excerpt: Chapter 7 ends with a five-item checklist. Here is how a small team can turn each item into one concrete action before the week ends.

source.title: Chapter 7 — Security, Identity, and High-Stakes Trust
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 7 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: By Friday, a small team can hold one page that answers five security questions about its agents. Chapter 7 ends with a practical checklist of five items. Each one fits in a week. None needs a new product. They need a few honest conversations and some edits to configuration.
Start with the agents you already run

First, check for the four-controls baseline. The chapter, citing Fouad Matin's guidance for coding agents at OpenAI, names them: sandboxing, network restriction, privilege boundaries, and human review. Each stops a different failure. Sit with one agent and mark which of the four it has. Treat any gap as a defect now, not as hardening for after an incident.

Second, run a survivability test at each step. The chapter says to build for "the agent will sometimes be wrong." So for each step, ask whether a mistake there is survivable before you ask whether the agent could make it. Write the answer next to the step. Where the answer is no, add a gate or narrow the power.

Third, write one default-permission row per agent. Skip the blanket policy. The chapter gives examples. A research agent may need no write access at all. A support agent may read account metadata but not issue refunds. A legal workflow may need broad retrieval but no authority to send anything externally. Set the minimum per stage of the workflow, not only per agent. A scope that looks harmless alone can compound once it pairs with retrieval, persistence, and retries.
Then look at connections and credentials

Fourth, apply the governance test before you add a tool server. The chapter says that if a new connection grows your agents' reach faster than your team can answer who can call this, with what scope, and where it is logged, standardization has expanded your attack surface. Make that a gate. No new server joins until someone writes down the three answers.

The chapter quotes Tun Shwe at Lenses: "Your insecure MCP server won't survive production." The failures he points to are mundane. Authentication gets treated as a configuration option. Tool descriptions get trusted as input. Servers go public because internal routing was harder.

Fifth, hunt for standing credentials. Search your agent configuration for long-lived API keys and for personal access tokens borrowed from an operator. The chapter calls a standing credential a red flag. An agent on a borrowed key does not hold delegated authority. It impersonates the operator, with no expiry and nothing to revoke. The chapter points toward a short-lived, scoped token bound to a session, a user, and a task.
A plan for the week

- Day one: list your agents. - Day two: mark which of the four controls each has. - Day three: write the permission rows. - Day four: review every connected tool server against the governance test. - Day five: replace one standing credential with a scoped one, and log what you could not fix yet.
You will not finish everything. That is fine. The checklist does not promise safety. It asks you to make carelessness less powerful, one agent at a time.

Friday's page holds three things: one permission row per agent, one answer to the three governance questions per tool server, and a short list of credentials still to replace. Print it and put it in the next sprint review.

title: The day a client disputes what the assistant filed
excerpt: A scene from Chapter 7 shows why audit trails matter as much as blocking bad actions, and what a partner can say when a client asks what happened.

source.title: Chapter 7 — Security, Identity, and High-Stakes Trust
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 7 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A client disputes a position that Hargrove's assistant helped file. A partner must answer one question: what did the system actually do? Chapter 7 uses this scene to teach one lesson about trust, and the lesson is not about prevention.
Two possible answers

In the first version, the assistant reached its documents through a mediation layer. The answer exists. The trajectory shows which matter files the assistant retrieved, which validation engine it called, and which draft it surfaced. It also shows the authority behind each step. The assistant worked under a read-only token scoped to this matter. It had no authority to send anything to the client.
In the second version, nothing was recorded. The chapter is direct about this case. Without a trail, the honest answer would be a shrug. The firm would hold a liability it cannot bound.

That contrast carries the lesson. Security talk often centers on blocking bad actions. The chapter says blocking is only half the requirement. In high-stakes work, trust also depends on reconstructing what happened. Which sources were consulted? Which tool calls were made? Which permissions were exercised? Which output reached review, and by what path? If a regulator asks later, the organization needs more than a statement that the model was generally aligned. It needs evidence.
What the trail does

The chapter treats observability as part of the security argument, not a side topic. Rich traces, approval logs, trajectory views, and reviewable histories let an institution turn bounded autonomy into something it can defend.

The chapter draws on Joel Hron's high-stakes framing. The answer there is not unrestricted autonomy under perfect prevention. It is constrained execution plus inspectable paths. The system does meaningful work and leaves a trail that domain experts can examine.

Look at how the scene depends on earlier design choices. The read-only, matter-scoped token is least privilege. The mediation layer made the trail possible in the first place. The partner can answer calmly because the architecture was built to be questioned.
The tension the chapter admits

Inspection has a cost. Detailed traces can expose sensitive data, internal reasoning artifacts, or privileged content. A trail that anyone can read becomes its own risk. So the chapter asks for selective retention, role-based visibility, redaction strategies, and separate surfaces for operators, reviewers, and auditors. The tension does not argue against inspection. It argues for governing inspection properly.
The takeaway
Ask the partner's question about your own agent. If a client or a regulator asked what it did last Tuesday, could you name the sources it consulted, the tools it called, and the permissions it used?
If you could not, start with the cheapest fix. Pick one agent and record, for each run, the tool calls and the authority used. Then decide who may read that record, and write that down too.

title: Voice is a stress test for the whole agent system
excerpt: Text chat hides latency, awkward pauses and weak handoffs. Chapter 8 argues that voice removes that cover and shows whether the loop around the model is sound.

source.title: Chapter 8 — Realtime, Voice, and the Cost of Being Interruptible
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 8 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A chat window hides a slow agent behind a blinking cursor. A phone call does not. Chapter 8 of the book builds its argument on that gap.

Text chat flatters AI systems. It tolerates awkward pauses. It lets a weak handoff look like thoughtful reflection. Users scroll, reinterpret and quietly repair what the system failed to make clear. Much fragile AI feels smarter in text because text is forgiving.
Voice removes that mercy. The chapter's claim: voice shows whether the rest of the architecture was honest.
Voice strips away excuses
The chapter says the field treats voice as a charming frontier, a natural interface that needs slightly better models. It calls that framing too soft. Voice matters because it takes away the excuses.

- Weak context architecture: the system fumbles the thread. - Brittle runtime: interruptions break it. - Sloppy security model: approvals turn casual and authority turns ambient. - Underdesigned control plane: the user rescues the interaction again and again. - Slow tool layer: the product sounds incompetent, however good the core model is.

Earlier chapters covered scaffolding, evals, context, runtime design, authority boundaries and human control. Realtime compresses all of them into milliseconds. Problems that chat hides become audible. Kwindla Hultman Kramer draws the line by the clock. Real time, he says, is anything inside "conversational latency of a few hundred milliseconds or less."
Where the test lives

Speech recognition and speech synthesis are not the hard part. The chapter names a narrower test: timing, overlap and interruption. These are the three ways a live conversation breaks. Even as speech models improve, systems still wait too long, cut in too aggressively, or lose the thread when the human changes direction mid-sentence.

A model can speak perfectly and still fail all three. The test asks whether the system can coordinate listening, reasoning, tool use and speaking under live pressure. That is a property of the loop around the model. The model alone does not decide it.

So the chapter calls a realtime system the most unforgiving version of a general truth: trustworthy AI depends on the loop around the model. Voice makes the loop visible because the human is still in the room. The caller feels every systems defect as behavior. They hear the hesitation.
What changes in practice

The chapter points teams at a different question. When a voice agent feels bad, do not reach first for a better voice or a bigger model. Ask which layer failed: context, runtime, authority, control or a slow tool.

The chapter adds that teams who think they are building a speech product often find they are building an orchestration product. Low latency depends on pipeline design, caching, asynchronous tool behavior and clean state handoff, as much as on model speed.
The chapter closes on three short lines:
Dependable AI is not merely a property of good answers. It is a property of good loops. And realtime interaction is where that truth becomes impossible to ignore.
Try it

Take the last voice failure your team logged. Write it down as a failure of a layer, not of the model. Name the layer: context, runtime, authority, control or tool. Then fix that layer first. The chapter's logic says the repair will also help your text chat, which only looked fine because nobody was listening for the delay.

title: Five voice agent changes a team can try this week
excerpt: Chapter 8 ends with five practical rules for realtime agents. Here is a day-by-day plan to apply each one this week without rebuilding your stack.

source.title: Chapter 8 — Realtime, Voice, and the Cost of Being Interruptible
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 8 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Your voice agent has a number that matters more than its average latency: the P95 from the caller's voice to the agent's voice. Chapter 8 ends with five rules. Each one fits into a day of work.
Monday: measure the whole loop
The first rule says to spend the latency budget on first audio, not on silence. A quick spoken acknowledgment followed by a slower answer beats a long silent pause followed by a polished one.

Start with measurement. Neil Zeghidour at Gradium AI puts the target for natural conversation at "around 200 milliseconds" for the entire stack of understanding, producing an answer, and pronouncing it. Kwindla Hultman Kramer says to watch the tail. In his words, "you care a lot if your P95 goes up above 800, 900, 1,000 milliseconds for the entire voice-to-voice response chain."

Record your own voice-to-voice P95. Then list your slowest tools. The chapter warns that tool calls become the bottleneck as speech layers improve. Zeghidour says a tool call runs "between 500 milliseconds and 4 seconds," and a 4-second pause is a dead line.
Tuesday: add acknowledgments
Put a short spoken acknowledgment in front of every slow step. Measure again. Streaming partial understanding can rescue a system whose deeper reasoning takes longer.
Wednesday: match the flow, then tighten confirmations

The second rule concerns half-duplex systems. Most production speech-to-speech systems cannot listen and speak at once. Structured, turn-based flows survive that limit. Open-ended companion chat does not, because the model reads every interjection as a barge-in. Decide which kind of flow your agent serves. If it is open-ended, narrow it. Do not patch the limit with longer silence thresholds.

The third rule inverts confirmation cost on purpose. The warmer the interface, the cheaper approval feels. Rank your agent's actions by consequence. For the top few, make confirmation deliberate: repeat the key detail back and ask for a clear yes. Keep low-stakes actions light.
Thursday: reuse the agent you trust

The fourth rule says to wrap voice around your strongest existing agent and not rebuild one. Luke Harries at ElevenLabs says the eval work is the asset to preserve, so the move is to "wrap it up into its own first-class primitive." Keep the tools, the evals and the workflow logic. If the underlying system is weak, voice exposes that faster. Run your existing evals against the core agent before you add the voice layer, and fix what fails.
Friday: voice the uncertainty

The fifth rule asks for a way to admit uncertainty out loud. In voice the human watches the system hesitate in real time. Write three spoken phrases: one to clarify, one to confirm, one to hand off. Then check that a real escalation path exists behind the third.
The takeaway
Know your voice-to-voice P95. Never leave the caller in silence while a slow step runs. Do the first part on Monday morning.

title: When a caller interrupts, your runtime gets tested
excerpt: A support-call scene from Chapter 8 shows that interruption handling is about execution semantics, not UX polish, and what to design for.

source.title: Chapter 8 — Realtime, Voice, and the Cost of Being Interruptible
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 8 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A caller is halfway through a sentence when they change the facts. The agent has already started a retrieval step. Chapter 8 uses this moment to teach one lesson: turn-taking is a runtime problem wearing a UX costume.

The chapter sets the scene with Hargrove's assistant, the running example in the book. It sits on a live support call. The client's account is locked. The case crosses billing and compliance rules. The client's patience is running out in real time. The agent must understand messy speech, notice that the caller interrupted to add a crucial exception, retrieve the right policy, check the client record, decide whether to act or escalate, and explain what it is doing. It must also avoid sounding lost or overconfident.
Where the call breaks
The chapter picks out several moments. Each one tests a different part of the system.

- The caller corrects their own account number halfway through a sentence. The system has to revise state. - The caller says, "No, wait, that was the old policy." The system has to tell abandoned context from active context. - The agent announces a short wait while it checks, then goes silent. The caller does not feel a neutral backend delay. The caller feels incompetence.

Then comes the hardest case. The agent has already begun a retrieval step when the caller reveals that the account belongs to a different region. If the runtime cannot cancel, redirect or downgrade the old plan cleanly, the agent starts answering with stale assumptions. The human hears a conversational failure. The root problem is execution semantics.
Questions that belong to the runtime
It is tempting to file interruption handling under experience polish. The chapter calls that too shallow. When a human cuts the system off, ask:

- What state is preserved? - Which partial output is discarded? - Does a tool call continue in the background? If so, how does the result surface later? - If the user answers a question indirectly, how much of the prior plan stays binding? - If a user correction and a returning tool result arrive together, which one takes priority?

The chapter says these are execution questions, not copywriting questions. They resemble the questions you ask of any durable workflow, now asked under a clock. A spoken system manages state in public. It needs a runtime that can pause, redirect, summarize and resume without forcing the user to rebuild everything by hand.

Security boundaries must also survive the change of medium. A friendly voice does not make overscoped authority less dangerous. Because voice feels human, people approve more casually. So the more consequential the action, the more deliberate the confirmation has to be.
Try it

Write the support-call script for your own agent. Include a mid-sentence correction, an abandoned policy and a late discovery that changes the plan while a retrieval step runs. Walk each case through your runtime on paper. For each one, write down three things: what state is kept, what is discarded and what the caller hears. Every blank answer marks a runtime gap. Fix it in the execution layer before you touch the words the agent speaks.

title: AI moves the bottleneck from typing to judgment
excerpt: Count the AI seats and a company looks transformed. Chapter 9 asks a harder question: did a single approval path change? Scarcity moves up, and work must follow.

source.title: Chapter 9 — The AI-Native Organization
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 9 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Count the AI seats and a company looks transformed. Now ask whether a single approval path has changed. Often it has not.

Chapter 9 of the book opens with this gap. Many adoption stories start small. Someone buys a seat. A few engineers get faster. A product manager drafts more quickly. Support summarizes tickets with less effort. These gains are real. They are also tool-use stories: local acceleration, not institutional redesign.
The chapter makes a different case. The biggest gains come from redesigning the organization so delegated machine work compounds instead of colliding.
Scarcity moves upward

AI does more than speed up output. It changes where scarcity lives. Execution gets cheaper. Exploration gets faster. More people can create artifacts that once needed a specialist. One operator can direct several agents in parallel.

Then new bottlenecks appear. Review load rises. Duplicate work spreads. Private agent workflows drift away from shared priorities. Standards get harder to enforce informally. Managers can no longer assume the org chart shows who can produce what.
So scarcity moves upward. It moves from typing to judgment, from production labor to orchestration, and from drafting to deciding which draft deserves trust.

The chapter states the rule plainly. More output per person is not the same as more throughput. An organization can produce far more while moving slower. When generation is nearly free, value does not vanish. It relocates, from making things to deciding which of them deserve trust.
Why access is not enough

A company can buy licenses and encourage experiments and still stay structurally unchanged. Individuals get a little faster. Decisions, approvals and responsibility flow through the same assumptions as before.

The chapter points to a threshold beyond access. Dan Shipper, who is building the AI-native company Every, puts it as a provocation: "There is a 10x difference between an organization where 90% of engineers use AI versus one where 100% do." The chapter reads the last ten percent as the point where compounding appears. Once use is pervasive, documentation quality matters more. Examples, standards, prompts and policies start to act as leverage.
The company as a harness

Earlier in the book, a harness is the environment built around a model so its work can be trusted. At company scale, the same idea means standards, specs, permissions, review rules and approved workflows, all written down. Humans and agents then work inside them.
Management stops inspecting every artifact. It designs the environment in which good artifacts are more likely to appear.

The chapter defines an AI-native organization as one that reorganized itself so machine-amplified work becomes cumulative instead of chaotic. Heavy AI use alone does not qualify. The strongest companies will be the ones that learned to convert cheap generation into trusted throughput.
Run the audit

The chapter ends its argument with a list: broader creation, tighter review, earlier alignment, stronger internal platforms, clearer authority boundaries, and operating models that treat delegated work as organizational material.

Read that list as an audit. For each item, ask one question. Does it exist as a written artifact that someone owns, or only as a habit in people's heads? A written rule compounds. A habit evaporates the moment its owner is busy.
Pick the item where the answer is "habit." Write it down this week, and give it an owner.

title: Five checks to run on your AI-native team this week
excerpt: Chapter 9 ends with five checks that need no new tool. Here is how a team can turn each one into a concrete step within a single week.

source.title: Chapter 9 — The AI-Native Organization
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 9 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Five checks. One week. No new tools. Chapter 9 closes with a checklist that asks a team to look at how work moves, not how much work gets made. Here is one way to run each item.
Find the queue and read your rituals

Start with the queue. Find where work piles up waiting on a person. The chapter says that is where scarcity actually moved. It tells you where to invest, so you stop guessing who is slow. Ask each team one question: what is waiting for a human right now? Write down the answers. Review requests, unmade decisions and unchecked drafts are the usual suspects.

Next, check what each ritual rations. A standup that reports how much got produced rations the abundant resource. A standup that surfaces which decisions are unmade rations the scarce one. The chapter says to run the second kind. Change one agenda this week. Replace the output round with a list of decisions waiting on someone.
Name owners and measure outcomes

Third, name the owner before you widen who can create. The chapter supports broader creation. Support teams, product managers and domain experts should be able to ship meaningful changes. But every path you open needs four answers:
- Who owns the production path? - Who owns domain correctness? - Who owns the security boundaries? - Which workflows stay human-gated?
Decide this before the path opens. Otherwise you discover the gap after something ships.

Fourth, measure outcomes, not artifact volume. The chapter names three numbers: rework rate, the share of generated work that ships unreverted, and time in the review queue. Pull them for one team. A dashboard that only counts pull requests can go green while the real constraint breaks. The chapter cites Nick Arcolano's analysis at Jellyfish, built on some twenty million pull requests, as the failure mode at scale. Output volume rises and the dashboards light up green. Whether the organization can review, integrate and trust that output goes unmeasured until it breaks.
Check that your voters are independent

The fifth check applies when you use redundancy to judge output. Majority voting and model debate can beat one expensive call. The chapter describes sampling several responses and voting, and having weaker models debate what a stronger model says. But the voters must be genuinely independent. One model sampled five times cancels noise. It does not cancel its shared blind spot. If your review setup samples one model repeatedly, add a voter that can disagree for different reasons.
Put it on one page
List the five checks on one page and give each to one person. By Friday the page should hold five things:
1. A list of queues. 2. One changed ritual. 3. A named owner for each widened path. 4. Three outcome numbers. 5. A verdict on whether your redundancy is real.
The chapter calls review capacity the control system for organizations that use agents. This page is a small version of it.
A week will not fix everything. It will show where your institution runs on habit instead of written rules. Start with the first gap on the page.
