title: A Monday morning at Meridian, and the coherence problem
excerpt: A staff engineer returns to twelve pull requests and no reckless act. The scene in Chapter 9 shows why output is no longer the scarce thing.

source.title: Chapter 9 — The AI-Native Organization
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 9 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: On Monday morning, a staff engineer at Meridian opens twelve pull requests, four synthetic eval reports and two security review requests. Nobody did anything wrong. That is the point of the scene in Chapter 9.

Meridian is a company well past casual AI adoption. Over the weekend, engineers launched subagents against backlog items. Product used internal tools to spin up three alternative flows for a new onboarding step. Support found a recurring customer complaint and had an agent draft both a help-center update and a proposed product fix.

A dashboard then showed that an internal automation had quietly touched three systems nobody had discussed together on Friday. Any one of them could be hiding another admin-override regression, the throttle on the wrong path from Chapter 4, now buried under a weekend of green checkmarks.
No reckless act
Read the scene again. Each move is locally defensible. Everyone is productive. The chapter says that is the problem.

Meridian is no longer starved for output. It is starved for coherence. Which changes matter? Which are duplicates? Which artifacts reflect current strategy, and which reflect a private interpretation of it? Which outputs are safe to merge, safe to trial, safe to ignore, or dangerous to trust? Who is responsible for saying so when authorship is half human, half machine, and spread across several functions?

This is where the Software Factory stops being only a repo pattern. Earlier chapters showed a team turning a repo into an environment agents can use. Chapter 9 asks what happens next. Someone has to own the rules. Someone has to decide which patterns become standard. The factory becomes a company problem.
Put the questions in order

The chapter gives an order for the questions. Settle ownership first, because every other question needs someone empowered to answer it. Then ask about strategy fit, which discards whole branches cheaply. Ask about safety-to-merge last. It is the expensive per-artifact check, so run it last and least.

Apply that order to the staff engineer's Monday. Without it, twelve pull requests and two security requests become fourteen separate inspections. With it, the first question is who owns each item. The second removes work that does not fit the current plan. Only the survivors earn the costly review.

The chapter names the cost of skipping this order alignment debt. It builds up when execution fans out faster than shared understanding. It comes due as rework, confusion, or an exhausting burst of manual coordination. The remedy is not to ban private leverage. Move alignment earlier, with shared planning, visible decomposition and common review spaces.
Try it on your own Monday

If your team already runs agents on weekends, do a short exercise. Imagine your next Monday. List what would be waiting for you. For each item, write down three things: who owns it, whether it fits the strategy, and what check would make it safe to merge.
Every blank in that list marks a place where your coherence will break first. Fill the blanks before the weekend.

title: What endures in AI engineering is constrained delegation
excerpt: Frameworks, models and interfaces will keep changing. Chapter 10 argues that one pattern for turning machine capability into dependable work will last.

source.title: Chapter 10 — What Endures
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 10 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Omar Khattab built systems, DSPy among them, across years of model turnover. Chapter 10 reports his verdict: they "fundamentally stayed the same over the years," from text-davinci-002 up to o4-mini. The models underneath were swapped out entirely. The structure stayed.

That fact frames the chapter's question. Agent frameworks multiply. Tool protocols proliferate. New releases reorder yesterday's leaderboard. Interfaces move from chat windows to canvases to copilots to swarms. Some of that is real progress. The chapter calls some of it marketing theater with a GPU budget. So what endures?
The chapter's answer is not a framework, a model family or an orchestration fashion. It is a pattern for turning machine capability into dependable work.
The pattern has a name

The chapter calls it constrained delegation. The machine gets a prepared environment, a clearer representation of intent and a workable slice of context. It gets a runtime that can preserve and expose state. Its authority matches the risk. Human review sits where it matters most.

The chapter also defines the pattern by what it excludes: raw generation, autonomous theater, tool sprawl disguised as capability, infinite context pretending to be memory, and a leaderboard screenshot standing in for product trust.

The chapter says the pattern will outlast today's frameworks and likely today's interface assumptions. The reason is simple. The pattern does not work around weak models. It answers the nature of delegated work itself.
Look past the interface

The visible part of a system is not the stable part. A coding agent does not earn trust with a polished diff view. A realtime voice system does not earn trust with natural speech. The question underneath is the same each time: what must be true around the model for delegated work to deserve trust?

The chapter's answer is the environment. Prepared repositories, specs, validations, retrieval systems, memory layers, runtimes, permissions and review surfaces are not accessories. They are how intelligence becomes situated. What endures, the chapter says, is not prompt cleverness but environment design.

Stronger models did not remove this work. They moved it. The chapter says teams that expected better models to dissolve complexity found it migrating into context assembly, eval design, runtime semantics, authority boundaries and organizational throughput. The model grew more capable. The loop around it grew more consequential.

The chapter also rejects the maximalist story of full autonomy. The most useful systems in the book were rarely the ones with the least human involvement. They were the ones with the clearest handoffs. Autonomy is a variable to tune, not a trophy.
Run the strike-out test
Take the plan for your next AI project. Strike out every model name and product name. Read what remains.

Does the plan still name a prepared environment, explicit intent, bounded authority and focused review? Then it rests on the parts the chapter calls durable. Does nothing remain? Then the plan depends on a moment, and the next release may end it.
Do this on the plan that sits open on your desk today. Rewrite one line that names a product so it names the constraint instead.

title: A week of work toward constrained delegation
excerpt: Chapter 10 closes with five practical steps. Here is how a team can run the diagnostic, set an autonomy dial and name an owner in one week.

source.title: Chapter 10 — What Endures
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 10 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Monday morning, a delegated system misbehaves. Someone suggests a bigger model. Chapter 10 closes with a checklist that starts by stopping that suggestion. Constrained delegation, the chapter says, is built one layer at a time, not declared all at once. Here is a week that builds one layer.
Diagnose before you upgrade

Pick the delegated system that misbehaves right now. Before anyone reaches for a bigger model, name which of six layers failed. The layers are legibility, evals, context, runtime, authority and supervision.

The chapter's logic runs down the chain. A legible workplace without evals is not enough. Evals without good context are not enough. Context without a durable runtime is not enough. Runtime without bounded authority is not enough. Security without usable supervision is not enough.

Hold a thirty-minute review with the people who saw the failure. Go through the six layers in order. Ask of each one: did it hold? Write the answer in one sentence. In the two recurring cases the book followed, the model was rarely the layer that failed. Your case may differ. The exercise makes you check before you spend.
Set the dial in writing

Choose one real workflow. Set its autonomy dial on paper. The chapter takes the dial from Joel Hron, who described treating agency this way: turn it up where the work is reversible and recoverable, turn it down where a wrong move costs something you cannot get back.
Write three lines for that workflow. What may the agent do alone? What needs a human? Why? The chapter's warning is blunt. An undocumented dial is a dial nobody actually set.
Name the owner

Before you ship, write down who is accountable for the system's output. The chapter asks for this before something breaks, not after. If no name comes to mind, nobody holds the responsibility yet. Write the name next to the workflow. This takes five minutes.
Build one thing

Now find the gap that hurts most and build one piece to close it. The chapter offers a menu: a legible repo, a real eval slice, a working set instead of a document dump, a durable runtime, a bounded credential, a control plane, a named owner. Pick one. Scope it to this week. The chapter says "one thing," so resist doing three.
Set a six-month reminder
Put a date in your calendar six months out. On that day, reread the seven "make" lines that end the chapter:

- Make the task legible. - Make the standards explicit. - Make the context usable. - Make the runtime durable. - Make authority narrow enough to trust. - Make review proportionate to risk. - Make the organization capable of learning.
The chapter sets the bar for the whole book here. The test is not whether you agreed with it. The test is whether more of those seven lines are true of your system than are true today.
So score yourself today. Mark each line true or false for your system, and save the page. In six months, the comparison will be honest because the first score is on paper.

title: What remains human is responsibility, not typing
excerpt: Chapter 10 argues the lasting human role in AI work is responsibility. A six-month test shows whether you have actually assigned it.

source.title: Chapter 10 — What Endures
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 10 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Picture a delegated system six months after launch. Its output turns out to be wrong. The person who wrote the prompt moved to a different team long ago. Who answers for the error?
Chapter 10 uses this scene as a test. If no name comes to mind, the chapter says, the responsibility was never assigned. It evaporated along with the context window that produced the output.
The shallow debate
The test sits inside a larger argument about what remains human. The chapter calls one version of that debate shallow: the version that fixates on which tasks people will keep doing by hand.

Humans may type less. They may implement less boilerplate. They may supervise parallel flows of machine work, edit generated artifacts, compose systems from agentic parts and step in mostly at moments of ambiguity or consequence. The chapter accepts all of that. It says none of it is the deeper role.
Five responsibilities
The deeper role is responsibility. The chapter lists what it covers:

- Responsibility for standards. - Responsibility for scoping. - Responsibility for the boundaries within which machines act. - Responsibility for deciding when evidence is sufficient. - Responsibility for noticing when the system is producing motion without progress.

The last item shows why a machine cannot hold the role. A system that generates a lot of work looks busy. Someone must judge whether the work moved anything. A machine can report its own activity. It cannot answer for it.

This follows a theme from earlier in the chapter. Cheap generation shifts value upward, toward framing, discrimination, prioritization and the willingness to throw away seductive garbage. As output gets cheaper, standards do not become quaint. They become load-bearing. The people who hold those standards do the human work, even when they never touch a keyboard.
Why one name is a hard test
The six-month test is hard to dodge because it does not ask whether your team cares about quality. It asks for a single answer. A team or a role will not pass it. A name will.

The chapter draws a wider conclusion from this. It stays skeptical of both utopian and defensive stories. AI neither leaves engineering unchanged nor removes the need for engineers. It relocates value toward those who can design, govern and continuously improve systems of delegated work.
Run the test today

Pick one workflow where an agent produces output that others rely on. Imagine it is six months from now and the output is wrong. Write down the name of the person who answers for it. Use a person, not a team.
If you cannot write a name, treat that gap as engineering work, due before the next feature. If you can, write the name where the next reader of the system will see it.
